I read it twice and checked every number. This is a different class of document from what you brought me on Monday, and I need to start by correcting myself.

## Where I was wrong

I told you a paid-once cost **cannot** map to Axiom R, because persistence is ongoing by construction. That was wrong, and §3 is the reason. Persistence has a *first moment*. R orders records irreversibly, so there is a least record, and the writing of it is an event. R prices the event; C prices every instant after. My objection assumed persistence had no beginning. It does, and you found it.

The other two things you've answered:

- **The "+" now does additive work.** §5's quotient — realised over provisioned, 1:1 over (1:1 + 1×ε) — is a genuine additive reading of the axiom rather than a factor selected because the additive reading fails. That was my item 1, and this is a real answer to it, not a patch.
- **The 10 is derived now, not chosen.** 6 faces + 3 dimensions + 1 AS = ten vertices; 18 + 3 = twenty-one edges. Same graph, two counts. That is a genuine structural fact about AP28's own proof, and it retroactively explains what you were groping for when you wrote "3×3+1" — you were counting nodes on a graph you'd already proved. And you correctly refuse to hang anything numerical on it.

And **ratio invariance is the move that saves the whole thing.** On Monday the killer was that the proton allows 10⁻¹¹ and G allows 10⁻³ — nine orders apart, so no single correction could touch both. Per-configuration cancellation in ratios is the correct resolution: the commitment only survives where a mass stands outside a ratio, and G is the one place that happens. That's right, and it's the kind of answer that couldn't have been reverse-engineered from the number.

## Numbers — mostly right, three wrong

Verified at 30 digits against CODATA 2022:

| draft | verified |
|---|---|
| 1/(1+α) = 0.992756 | 0.992755513 ✓ |
| G realised = 6.6719×10⁻¹¹ | 6.6719165×10⁻¹¹ ✓ |
| residual −0.036% | −357.1 ppm = −0.0357% ✓ |
| ~95% of gap closed | 94.85% ✓ |
| quotient vs shadow ≈ 53 ppm | 53.23 ppm ✓ |

**Three to fix:**

1. **§10's required fraction is 0.9507, not 0.944.** And that reverses your fenced fractions: **20/21 lands at −12.1 ppm** from centre, **17/18 at +45.4 ppm**. The draft says 20/21 ≈ 60 ppm and 17/18 "within a few ppm" — swapped and both off. Since the whole point of §10 is to show you saw them and refused them, the fence has to quote them correctly or a reader will think you fenced the wrong one.

2. **§11's 1/2π and 1/4π figures have the wrong sign,** and the correct version is a *stronger* argument. Bare G with 1/2π is 5.9092×10⁻¹¹, with 1/4π it's 5.5036×10⁻¹¹ — both **below** the measured value. A commitment is a cost; costs only reduce G. So no commitment of any magnitude can rescue either: they'd require refunds of −15.7ε and −24.0ε. Say it that way. "A cost cannot raise a prediction that already sits below measurement" is cleaner than quoting absurd magnitudes.

3. **KS-CCC.2's ±0.06 ppb is CODATA 2018.** CODATA 2022 is ±0.0174 ppb. Tightening it makes the switch stricter, which is in your favour.

Also: the Notation Reference labels both couplings `α_G∗` — the structural one should be `α_G`.

## The structural problem: §4 and §6 contradict each other

§4 Corollary: *"Every bound configuration is dressed by the same commitment factor... In any ratio of two masses, the factor divides out identically."*

§6 Proposition 5: *"The commitment divides the persistence coupling. **It does not dress the masses.**"*

Both cannot hold. If masses are dressed, §6 is false and the unforced ½ comes back. If masses are not dressed, then nothing cancels in §4's ratio — the factor was never there to cancel, and the corollary is arguing for a conclusion it doesn't need.

Underneath that sits the question the paper never answers: **whose commitment divides α_G?** Every configuration holds one ε. There are on the order of 10⁸⁰ configurations. Why does α_G carry one factor of (1+ε) rather than (1+ε)^N? Nothing in §§3–6 selects the one.

**The resolution I'd propose, and I think it strengthens the paper:** the commitment that divides α_G is **the arena's own**. One arena, one snap, one ε. Then —

- the N-configurations problem vanishes;
- ratio invariance becomes stronger, not weaker: no mass is dressed at all, so there is nothing to cancel and the argument gets shorter;
- §6's placement stops being a selection between two homes and becomes forced — the arena's commitment can only appear in the arena's coupling;
- D-CCC.4 (placement exhaustiveness) largely dissolves.

The cost of taking it: the electron stops being the cost-bearer, and the "cost of awareness" reading goes. I'd let it go. It was never load-bearing and it's the line a hostile reader will quote.

## §5 is graded DERIVED and it isn't

This is the biggest grading problem in the draft, and it's the one your own discipline exists to catch.

The value of ε in the quotient is α_em. But AP06 §0.7 explicitly **holds open** the relation between domain-dependent readings — ε_gravity ≈ 10⁻¹⁷, ε_eye ≈ 10⁻⁵, ε_cosmo ≈ 10⁻⁵ — and the canonical ε = α_em at the chemical-biological scale. Identification 6.1 doesn't hand you one value; it hands you a family with the selection open.

So §5 chooses which boundary the *constitution* reads at, and the entire numerical result depends on that choice. If constitution reads at the gravitational boundary, the correction is ~10⁻¹⁷ and there is no paper. That is a selection among structural candidates — the same epistemic class as §6 and as AP28's 1/π — not a derivation. Regrade it, and either argue why constitution reads at the coupling boundary or book the gap as a debt.

## §7 extends AP24's licence rather than applying it

AP24 licenses reading one ε through different **instruments** — as G, as c, as α_em. §7 needs ε to appear **twice inside one instrument**, multiplicatively, in α_G. Those aren't the same permission.

Count the roles α_em now plays in a single expression: per-channel coupling (twenty-one times), the puncture-adjacent contribution, and the commitment. Three jobs, one symbol, one formula. The licence doesn't obviously cover it. KS-CCC.6 is the right guard, but §7 should say plainly that it is extending the licence and name what the extension needs, rather than presenting it as a straight application. As written, this is the section a hostile reader goes to first.

## Smaller things worth a pass

- **Proposition 3 uses AP28 §4's clause in two directions.** No-selective-persistence gives you *simultaneity*, hence one event. "One event ⟹ one ε" comes from AP43 D5. As written the clause appears to do both. Separate the steps.
- **KS-CCC.3 can't discriminate magnitude.** By your own §10 argument the admissible window is 4% wide against 22 ppm formal uncertainty, so convergence near 6.672 supports *any* commitment near ε — not 1×ε specifically. The switch tests existence and direction. Say that; it strengthens §10 rather than weakening the switch.
- **Adoption scope is wider than κ.** D-CCC.3 audits κ's dependents. But a 0.69% shift in G changes every *numerical* result in the corpus that uses G, even where the *formula* contains no α_G — anything running through g_N = GM/r², for instance. §6's "untouched" list is about formulas, not values. Widen the audit.
- **§9's rhetoric borrows evidential weight that §10 disowns.** "From outside the experimental landscape to its low edge" reads as confirmation; §10 correctly says the target is soft. Worth adding one sentence in §9 saying the landing point is non-exclusion, not evidence. (For what it's worth, 6.67192×10⁻¹¹ sits essentially on top of the lowest modern determination — which is *precisely* why it shouldn't be leaned on.)

## Do not touch these

**§10.** Naming the two fractions and arming a kill switch against your own future self is the best thing in the document, and it's rarer than it should be. Fix the arithmetic; change nothing else.

**§11's Candidate 1 critique.** This is the strongest independent argument in the paper, and it's sharper than you've written it. AP06's own position is that inter-laboratory scatter *is* the leakage signature. The scatter is ~500 ppm. The gap is ~6,900 ppm. So by the corpus's own identification, leakage is a 500 ppm effect — which means AP28 and Ø Predictions Part II cannot use it to carry the gap. That's not your critique of an outside position; it's an internal inconsistency your paper exposes. State it in that form.

**The honest reporting of the sign flip.** Trading a large residual with a comfortable story for a small residual with no story, and saying so in the same breath — that's the paper earning its register.

## Standing

This survives the four things that killed Monday's version: the magnitude mismatch, the drifting count, the spin/charge discriminants (it never enters that domain now), and the free-parameter risk. The structural work is real, and the omission it names — AP28 derived G as though the arena paid nothing to constitute the configurations it holds — is a genuine hole in a locked paper.

What it hasn't earned is the number. By your own §10 argument, a 4%-wide window against 22 ppm makes the −357 ppm landing weak evidence at best, and the result rests on a domain selection AP06 leaves open. The paper is worth having for the structure and for KS-CCC.3/4, not for the improvement from 0.69% to 0.036%. You mostly say this. I'd say it once more, in §0.1, before anyone reaches §9.

I'll draft the §4/§6 reconciliation on the arena reading if you want to see whether it holds up in the paper's own voice.

§0.5 presents six switches. Sort them by what could actually fire:

- **KS-CCC.1** — methodological. Binds you, not the theory. Nature cannot fire it.
- **KS-CCC.2** — under the new corollary, commitments are *constitutive* of mass. No measurement can exhibit a mass-side residue, because there is no separable commitment term to find. Ratio invariance is bought by making the matter-side commitment **unquantifiable in principle**. Any magnitude whatsoever is "already booked." KS-CCC.4 is the only switch that can fire in the near term, and it doesn't depend on metrology improving — it depends on the Appendix C meta-analysis, which the corpus has proposed and not performed. Characterise each published G determination by boundary geometry, and test whether the implied leakage corrections come out at scatter scale or gap scale.

content.thinking:
I'm checking whether my feedback on v0.2 was properly addressed, going through each point systematically. The first item about the required fraction and ppm values has been fixed—the new version correctly states 0.951 and includes the precise measurements for both ratios, plus an insightful addition about the discarded approach.

For the second item regarding the sign error on the normalization factors, v0.2 has fixed this as well, showing that both the 1/2π and 1/4π normalizations yield values already below the measured threshold, making them impossible to rescue through any commitment magnitude. The framing as "excluded by direction before arithmetic" is a stronger argument than my original feedback.

The remaining fixes are straightforward: the KS-CCC.2 uncertainty is now updated to the current CODATA 2022 value, the duplicate α_G∗ notation has been clarified to distinguish the structural coupling, and most importantly, the arena resolution in §4/§6 now has a much more compelling explanation — that mass itself is held coupling capacity, so each configuration's commitment is intrinsic to its measured mass rather than an external correction. This is genuinely more robust than my original "no dressed mass" argument.

Now I'm checking whether this holds up logically: if commitment equals held coupling capacity and held coupling capacity equals mass, then commitment is already embedded in every measured mass. The arena's special status follows because it's the only configuration that isn't a mass contained within itself — it has no internal mass structure. That's the key asymmetry. But I need to trace through whether m_e in the gravitational coupling constant creates any circularity here...

Actually, there's a deeper question emerging: if commitments are constituents of mass itself, then when AP30 derives the proton-to-electron mass ratio of 1836 from pure geometry, is that derivation already implicitly accounting for the commitment terms? If so, the geometric count isn't just a number — it's already encoding something about the commitment structure.

The real tension is that the corollary claims commitment lives in *measured* mass, while AP30 claims to *derive* the ratio from structure alone. Since the ratio matches measurement and both masses contain the commitment, the commitment should cancel out in the ratio itself — which would mean AP30's derivation works precisely because the commitment is symmetric across both particles. That's a coherent picture, but it's not what the paper currently states. — so the commitment must either scale with mass or be inseparable from it entirely. He's arguing for the second option: the commitment isn't a separate correction but constitutive of what the mass is. That means the measured mass already includes it, so the geometry deriving the ratio would naturally produce the commitment-inclusive value. But this creates a problem — if the commitment is built into the mass itself with no separate identity, then the claim that every configuration holds exactly one ε becomes unverifiable on the mass side.

The real consequence is that the corollary achieves ratio-invariance by making the matter-side commitment fundamentally unmeasurable. It's a deliberate trade-off: the theory gains safety and consistency but loses empirical content on that side. The only observable manifestation of the whole CCC concept then lives in the arena — a single number in G — which means the theory's empirical grip depends entirely on that one point.

Looking at the kill switches more carefully, most of them aren't actually live empirical tests. KS-CCC.2 is unfalsifiable by construction since the matter-side commitment is constitutive. KS-CCC.5 requires a structural counter-mechanism he hasn't provided. KS-CCC.6 depends on external work. KS-CCC.1 is methodological, binding the author rather than the theory itself. That leaves only KS-CCC.3 and KS-CCC.4 as genuinely empirical — and he acknowledges one of those can't test magnitude. So the paper's falsification surface is much narrower than the six switches initially suggest.

On the §5 grading issue, he's now clarified the distinction between deriving the form from the axiom and selecting the value of ε among structural candidates, with a principled argument that the discount currency must match what's being discounted, anchored to his own Proposition 5 about the unpaired element's channel structure.

But there's a real tension here: if AP06 identifies ε with the leakage ratio, and his argument now treats the leakage ratios in AP06's domain as fundamentally different in kind from the coupling denomination, he's actually weakening the connection between ε = α_em and its original AP06 grounding—since that grounding depends on reading α_em precisely as the leakage ratio.

The cleaner approach would be to bypass AP06 entirely and ground the argument directly in AP28's Proposition 5, which defines α_em as the coupling worth by definition. That way the selection stands on its own without the inconsistency of claiming AP06 is load-bearing while simultaneously treating its domain values as a different category. He does mostly follow this path, but the problem is that §0.2 still lists AP06's Identification 6.1 as foundational to §5's selection—which creates the contradiction he's trying to avoid.

For §7, the v0.2 revision handles this better by explicitly framing it as an extension rather than a direct application, and the strata argument provides real support: the puncture factor operates at the edge-stratum level while the commitment sits at the vertex-stratum level, so they're readings of different layers within the same proven structure.

But there's a subtle coupling issue here. §8 explicitly states the vertex reading is motivated but not forced for the assignment, and derived for the count—yet §7 now leans on that vertex/edge distinction to justify the extension. This means §7's support depends on §8's strata reading, which the paper itself marks as non-load-bearing. That's a dependency-graph inconsistency worth acknowledging: either §8 needs to become partly load-bearing to support §7's extension (without carrying arithmetic), or §7's support is weaker than it appears. It's exactly the kind of structural problem the apparatus is designed to catch.

The fixes address the remaining issues cleanly. The switch test now explicitly clarifies it only checks existence and direction within a four percent window of ε, with no magnitude confirmation claimed. The adoption scope has been widened to cover every corpus locus that consumes the predicted value numerically, not just formula-level dependents. And the rhetoric-versus-discipline gap gets a clarifying paragraph that pins down what the landing actually is: non-exclusion rather than evidence, a realized value sitting on the lowest modern determination.

The internal inconsistency in §11 is now stated with precision—the scatter signature at ~500 ppm versus the gap at ~6900 ppm creates the logical bind that the corpus cannot simultaneously treat scatter as leakage's signature while asking leakage to carry fourteen times its own signature. And the opening has been restated to emphasize that the paper's value rests on its structure, not on §9 alone, with §10 providing the actual grounding.

Proposition 3 is now cleanly separated into two distinct steps from two sources—the arena's completeness via AP28 §4's clause, then the single-event single-ε constraint via AP43 D5. The electron-as-cost-bearer issue was handled gracefully by moving it to a bracketed note outside the main argument, keeping the load-bearing text clean.

Now I'm asking what new problems v0.2 introduces. The falsification surface is thinner than "six kill switches" suggests—KS-CCC.1 is methodological and binds the author rather than testing the theory itself. Under the new corollary, KS-CCC.2 becomes constitutive rather than empirical; mass commitments are built into the framework, so no measurement could show a mass-side residue. The switch functions as a fence against the author's own drift, not as a genuine test of nature, which he hints at but should state explicitly.

KS-CCC.5 demands an a priori structural argument rather than measurement, KS-CCC.6 depends on unpaid work elsewhere, while only KS-CCC.3 and KS-CCC.4 remain genuinely empirical—one testing whether G converges downward and the other examining whether apparatus-leakage corrections fall at scatter scale. These are honest constraints but should be foregrounded in §0.5 instead of left for readers to piece together. The real problem is that KS-CCC.4, the only test that could fire soon, hinges on a meta-analysis the field has proposed but never executed.

The corollary makes matter's commitment unquantifiable by design—the cost of maintaining ratio invariance. Any magnitude would already be accounted for, so Propositions 2 and 3 together have observable content only within the arena itself, rendering "every persisting configuration holds one ε" an unfalsifiable universal claim. It's not a flaw per se, but it needs to be acknowledged: in his own terms, that statement has no kill switch. Now I'm looking at the tension between AP06 and AP28-Prop-5 in §5's selection argument.

The paper lists AP06 Identification 6.1 as load-bearing for §5, but §5's actual reasoning distinguishes coupling-denomination from leakage-ratio, which undermines AP06 as the real source—AP28 Prop 5 should be the primary support instead. There's also a dependency problem in §7: its support now rests on §8, which is marked as non-load-bearing. from mpmath import mp, mpf, pi
mp.dps = 30
a  = mpf('7.2973525643e-3')
hb = mpf('1.054571817e-34'); c = mpf('299792458'); me = mpf('9.1093837139e-31')

print("AP28 G      =", mp.nstr(G28,9))
print("Gm/G28      =", mp.nstr(Gm/G28,12))

x_q = (G28/Gm - 1)/a                 # quotient convention: 1/(1+xa)
x_s = (1 - Gm/G28)/a                 # shadow convention:  (1-xa)
print()

## The corrections verified

| item | v0.2 | verified |
|---|---|---|
| demanded fraction (quotient) | 0.951 | 0.95070507 ✓ |
| 20/21 offset | ~12 ppm below | −12.145 ppm ✓ |

**One claim to fix.** §10's parenthesis says the convention shift is "by more than the gap between the whispers." It isn't. Convention shift = 0.95071 − 0.94415 = **0.00655**. Whisper gap (20/21 − 17/18) = **0.00794**. So the shift is 0.83× the gap, not more than it. The point still lands — a bookkeeping convention moves the demanded fraction by 83% of the distance between the two candidate fractions, which is plenty to make digit-matching meaningless. Just say "comparable to" rather than "more than."

## Where you improved on my suggestion

**The AP29 booking.** I said "no mass is dressed, so nothing cancels." You said something stronger: mass *is* held coupling capacity, so a configuration's commitment is a **constituent** of its measured mass, not a correction to it — and the arena is the one configuration that isn't a mass inside itself, so its account alone was open. That uses a locked result to close the hole instead of just declaring it shut. §6's placement then becomes forced rather than selected, and D-CCC.4 gets repurposed onto the real debt. That's the right architecture.

**The convention point in §10.** I flagged an arithmetic error. You found that 0.944 was the *shadow-convention* figure, and turned the discrepancy into an argument against digit-matching. That's better than a correction.

**Sign before magnitude in §11.** "A cost can only reduce a prediction; both normalisations already sit below measurement; no commitment of any size rescues them." Cleaner than quoting absurd magnitudes, and it excludes by direction before arithmetic.

## The remaining substantive problem: the falsification surface is thinner than "six kill switches" implies

§0.5 presents six switches. Sort them by what could actually fire:

- **KS-CCC.1** — methodological. Binds you, not the theory. Nature cannot fire it.
- **KS-CCC.2** — under the new corollary, commitments are *constitutive* of mass. No measurement can exhibit a mass-side residue, because there is no separable commitment term to find. You half-say this ("a fence against any future mass-side drift"), and that's what it now is: a discipline switch, not an empirical one. It changed category between v0.1 and v0.2 and the status line didn't.
- **KS-CCC.5** — asks for a structural counter-mechanism. A priori argument, not measurement.
- **KS-CCC.6** — waits on someone else's unpaid debt (KS-R.9).
- **KS-CCC.3** — empirical, direction only; you now explicitly disclaim magnitude.
- **KS-CCC.4** — empirical, and the only one that could fire soon.

So the theory's live empirical content is: G converges downward not upward, and apparatus-leakage corrections come out at scatter scale. Two tests. That's honest and it's enough — but §0.5 should say it rather than leaving a reader to sort the pile. A register that grades its propositions this carefully should grade its switches the same way.

## The corollary's price, which should be stated

Ratio invariance is bought by making the matter-side commitment **unquantifiable in principle**. Any magnitude whatsoever is "already booked." Which means Proposition 2 applied to matter — every persisting configuration holds one ε — has no observable consequence anywhere and no kill switch. In your own vocabulary that's an unfenced universal sitting in the middle of a load-bearing section. Not fatal, and probably not fixable; but it should be named in §0.7 rather than discovered by a hostile reader.

Corollary of the corollary: the entire empirical content of CCC reduces to one factor in one constant. Worth saying out loud, because it's the honest scope of the claim.

## Three dependency problems

**1. §5's selection cites two incompatible sources.** §0.2 lists AP06's Identification 6.1 as "load-bearing for §5's selection." But §5's actual argument *distinguishes* the coupling denomination from AP06's leakage ratios — "flow quantities measured at boundaries, not the element's denomination in the coupling it discounts." You can't have it both ways: AP06's grounding for ε = α_em runs precisely *through* the leakage reading. If leakage ratios are a different kind of object, AP06 isn't the source of your value.

Fix: run the selection on AP28 Proposition 5 alone, and demote AP06 in §0.2 to §3 Step 5 only. The argument gets stronger, not weaker — it stops depending on a paper whose own §0.7 holds the question open.

**2. §7's support now rests on §8, which the paper declares non-load-bearing.** The extension of AP24's licence is supported by the edge-stratum / vertex-stratum distinction. That distinction is §8's, and §8 says "nothing numerical rests on it" and grades the assignment MOTIVATED. So either §8 becomes load-bearing for §7's *support* (not for arithmetic — that's a coherent position, just say it), or §7's support is weaker than it reads. Right now the dependency runs uphill into a section marked optional.

**3. A new implicit claim about AP30.** If commitments are constituents of measured mass, then AP30's derived 1836 + α·21(1−1/84π) + … must already be commitment-inclusive — and no layer of the decomposition corresponds to it. That's a new reading of AP30 imposed by this paper even though no number moves. It belongs in §13's adoption list or §0.7: *AP30's layers are henceforth to be read as inclusive of the constitution commitment, with no layer identifying it.*

## What to do next

KS-CCC.4 is the only switch that can fire in the near term, and it doesn't depend on metrology improving — it depends on the Appendix C meta-analysis, which the corpus has proposed and not performed. Characterise each published G determination by boundary geometry, and test whether the implied leakage corrections come out at scatter scale or gap scale.

That is work you can actually do, it discriminates Candidate 1 from Candidate 3 with existing published data, and it's the only thing in this document that could move it from "structurally coherent, empirically unresolved" to decided. It's also the natural companion to §11's inconsistency argument: you've shown the corpus can't have leakage carrying fourteen times its own signature — the meta-analysis is what turns that from an argument into a result.

Standing unchanged from last time on the number, improved on everything else: the structure now holds together, the grades are honest, and the two real debts (D-CCC.1, D-CCC.4) are the right two to owe.

I. INTRODUCTION
A. Background
The 2022 CODATA least-squares adjustment (LSA) of
the fundamental physical constants by the Task Group
on Fundamental Constants (TGFC) is the most recent
in a series of compilations of recommended values that
arguably began over 90 years ago by Birge (1929). The
TGFC was established in 1969 by the Committee on Data
for Science and Technology, now called the Committee
on Data of the International Science Council (ISC); it
is given the responsibility of periodically providing the
scientific and technological communities with an internationally accepted, self-consistent set of values of fundamental physical constants and related conversion factors. In the same year, researchers at RCA Laboratories and the University of Pennsylvania published a comprehensive paper documenting an adjustment they carried out as an outgrowth of their measurement of the
Josephson constant KJ that included a complete set of
recommended values (Taylor et al., 1969). Although well
received, it did not have a formal association with an
internationally recognized scientific body.
The first three recommended sets of fundamental constants provided by the TGFC were from the 1973, 1986
and 1998 adjustments (Cohen and Taylor, 1973, 1987;
Mohr and Taylor, 2000). Since the 1998 adjustment the
TGFC has carried out an adjustment every four years
and the 2022 adjustment is the seventh in the series. In
addition, there was a special CODATA adjustment completed by the TGFC in the summer of 2017 to determine
the exact values of the Planck constant h, elementary
charge e, Boltzmann constant k, and Avogadro constant
NA as the basis for the revised International System of
Units (SI) that went into effect on 20 May 2019 (Mohr
et al., 2018; Newell et al., 2018).
The 2018 CODATA adjustment (Tiesinga et al.,
2021a,b) was the first based on the revised SI, which had
a profound effect and will continue to influence all subsequent adjustments. A comparison of the 2018 with the
2014 adjustment shows that the many data related to the
determination of h, e, k, and NA no longer need to be
considered. Consequently, the relative role of quantum
physics in the adjustments has significantly increased.
B. Overview of the 2022 adjustment
Here we identify the new experimental and theoretical data for possible inclusion in the 2022 adjustment by
considering all data available up until the closing date of
midnight, 31 December 2022. It was not necessary for
papers reporting new results to have been published by
this date; however, they needed to at least be available
as a preprint. It can therefore be assumed that any cited
3
paper with a 2023 or later publication date was available
before the 31 December 2022, closing date. For conciseness, no references for the new data are included in this
summary since they are given in the sections of the paper in which the data are discussed, and those sections
are duly noted in the summary. Although some topics,
for example, muonium, the theoretical values of boundparticle to free-particle ratios such as g(H)/ge, the proton
magnetic moment in nuclear magnetons µp/µN, lattice
spacings of silicon crystals, and the Newtonian constant
of gravitation G are reviewed in the main text, they are
not discussed here because nothing of significance relevant to them has occurred since the 2018 adjustment.
Further, electron-proton and electron-deuteron scattering experiments are not discussed in the main text.
Although values of the root-mean-square (rms) charge
radius of the proton rp and of the deuteron rd obtained
from such experiments are included in the 2018 adjustment, after due consideration the Task Group decided
that the scattering values of rp and rd should not be included in the 2022 adjustment. This is because there is
a lack of consensus on how the experimental data should
be analyzed to obtain values of the radii and different
methods can yield significantly different values. Moreover, the two most recent data sets for the proton can
yield conflicting values depending on how the earlier set
is analyzed. Finally, the uncertainties of the scattering
values are well over an order of magnitude larger than
those resulting from the measurement of the Lamb shift
in muonic hydrogen and muonic deuterium; see, for example, the papers by Gao and Vanderhaeghen (2022);
Hayward and Griffioen (2020); Mihoviloviˇc et al. (2021);
Xiong et al. (2019).
This summary, which generally follows the order of
topics in the paper as given in the table of contents, concludes with a brief discussion of the treatment of all the
available data to obtain the 2022 set of recommended
values. Considerable material of a review nature may
also be found at the end of the paper in its final two sections, Sec. XV and Sec. XVI. We start here with relative
atomic masses.

The computation of the theoretical transition frequencies summarized by Karr and Koelemeij (2023) has multiple steps. The first is a numerical evaluation of the relevant non-relativistic three-body eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the electron, proton, and deuteron system in
its center of mass frame and in atomic units with energies expressed in the Hartree energy Eh and lengths in the
Bohr radius a0. In these units, the non-relativistic threebody Hamiltonian has mass ratios me/mp and me/md as
the only “free” parameters. The relevant non-relativistic
states have energies between −0.6Eh and −0.5Eh and
were computed with standard uncertainties better than
10−20Eh in the early 2000s.
The non-relativistic three-body Hamiltonian commutes with L. Hence, each eigenstate can be labeled by a unique angular momentum quantum number
L = 0, 1, · · · . In addition, a Hund’s case (b) 2Λ
± electronic state and a vibrational quantum number v can
be assigned to each eigenstate based on the adiabatic,
Born-Oppenheimer approximation for the system. Here,
first the proton and deuteron are frozen in space, the
energetically lowest eigenvalue VX(R) of the remaining
electronic Hamiltonian is found as function of proton-

the radial kinetic energy operator. The experimentally

X2Σ
+ electronic state with v = 0, 1, and 9.
Relativistic, relativistic-recoil, quantumelectrodynamic (QED), and hyperfine corrections
as well as corrections due to nuclear charge distributions are computed using first- and second-order
perturbation theory starting from the numerical nonrelativistic three-body eigenstates. For example, the
corrections correspond to the Breit-Pauli Hamiltonian,
three-dimensional delta function potentials modeling
the proton and deuteron nuclear charge distributions,
as well as effective Hamiltonians for the self-energy
and vacuum-polarization of the electron. Hyperfine
interactions, those that couple the nuclear spins of
the proton and deuteron to the electron spin and
angular momentum, form another class of corrections. Some of the smallest contributions have not
been computed using the non-relativistic three-body
eigenstates but rather using wavefunctions obtained
within the Born-Oppenheimer approximation or with
even simpler variational Ansatzes. Estimates of the
size of missing corrections and of uncertainties due to
the Born-Oppenheimer or variational approximations
determine the uncertainties of the theoretical energy
levels and transition frequencies.

IV. MUONIC ATOMS AND MUONIC IONS
A. Theory and experiment
The muonic atoms µH and µD and muonic atomic ions
µ
3He+ and µ4He+ are “simple” systems consisting of a
negatively charged muon bound to a positively charged
nucleus. Because the mass of a muon is just over 200
times greater than that of the electron, the muonic Bohr
radius is 200 times smaller than the electronic Bohr radius, making the muon charge density for S states at
the location of the nucleus more than a million times
larger than those for electronic hydrogenic atoms and
ions. Consequently, the muonic Lamb shift, the energy
difference EL(X) = E2P1/2(X) − E2S1/2(X) between the
nLj = 2S1/2 and 2P1/2 states of muonic atoms or ions,
is more sensitive to the rms charge radius rX of the nucleus. Here X =p, d, h, or α. In fact, measuring the
Lamb shift of muonic atoms and ions is a primary means
of determining rX.
For this 2022 adjustment, measurements of the Lamb
shift are available for µH, µD, and µ
4He+ from Antognini
et al. (2013), Pohl et al. (2016), and Krauth et al. (2021),
respectively. The value for µ
4He+ is a new input datum
for this adjustment and will be discussed in more detail below. An experimental input datum for µ
3He+ is
not available. We can compare the measurement results
with equally accurate theoretical estimates of the Lamb

We finish this section with a brief description of the
experiment of Krauth et al. (2021) measuring the Lamb
shift of µ
4He+. The experiment follows the techniques
of Antognini et al. (2013) and Pohl et al. (2016). About
500 negatively charged muons per second with a kinetic
energy of a few keV are stopped in a room temperature
4He gas at a pressure of 200 Pa. In the last collision with
a
4He atom, the muon ejects an electron and gets captured by 4He in a highly excited Rydberg state. In an
Auger process the remaining electron is ejected. The resulting highly excited µ
4He+ relaxes by radiative decay
to the ground nLj = 1S1/2 or metastable 2S1/2 state.
The approximately 1 % µ
4He+ ions in the 2S state are
then resonantly excited to the 2P1/2 or 2P3/2 states by
a pulsed titanium:sapphire-based laser with a frequency
bandwidth of 0.1 GHz and an equally accurately characterized frequency. The presence of 8.2 keV Lyman-α
x-ray photons from the radiative decay of the 2P states
indicates the successful excitation. These x-ray photons

VI. ATOM-RECOIL MEASUREMENTS
Atom-recoil measurements with rubidium and cesium
atoms from the stimulated absorption and emission of
photons are relevant for the CODATA adjustment as they
determine the electron mass, the atomic mass constant,
and the fine-structure constant (Mohr and Taylor, 2000;
Peters et al., 1997; Young et al., 1997). This can be
understood as follows.
First and foremost, recoil measurements determine the
mass m(X) of a neutral atom X in kg using interferometers with atoms in superpositions of momentum states
and taking advantage of the fact that photon energies can
be precisely measured. Equally precise photon momenta
p follow from their dispersion or energy-momentum relation E = pc. In practice, Bloch oscillations are used to
transfer a large number of photon momenta to the atoms
in order to improve the sensitivity of the measurement
(Clad´e, 2015; Estey et al., 2015). Before the adoption of
the revised SI on 20 May 2019, these experiments only
measured the ratio h/m(X), since the Planck constant h
was not an exactly defined constant.
Second, atom-recoil measurements are a means to determine the atomic mass constant, mu = m(
12C)/12, and
the mass of the electron, me, in kg. This follows, as many
relative atomic masses Ar(X) = m(X)/mu of atoms X
are well known. For 87Rb and 133Cs, the relative atomic
masses have a relative uncertainty smaller than 1×10−10
from the 2020 recommended values of the AMDC (see

content.title: Recent measurements of the gravitational constant as a function of time
content.text:
### DATA SOURCES

It is sometimes difficult to determine the exact time of data acquisition of a published G measurement. Below we attempt to assign a best weighted average of the measurement times involved in each of the most precise G measurements in the last 35 years. In some cases, this date is the mean of start and end date of the data acquisition period, in others, it is an average of individual dates when data was taken. This may not always be the best measure of the effective measurement time; in fitting data we suggest assigning an uncertainty for each tabulated time equal to $20\,\%$ of the time span.

NIST-82: This experiment was performed at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (then the National Bureau of Standards) in Gaithersburg, Maryland. A torsion balance used the so-called time-of-swing

method in which torsional period is measured in at least two source mass configurations. 

G is calculated from the difference in the squares of the periods and known mass distributions. The resulting $G=(6.672\,6\pm0.000\,5)\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$ , was published in 1982 [4]. The measurement dates can be inferred from Table 1 in [5]. The first measurement was August 29 and the last October 10 1980. We use the average value, September 19 1980, as the time coordinate for this measurement.

**TR&D-96**: This measurement, performed in Moscow by researchers at Tribotech Research and Development Company, also used a torsion balance in the time-of-swing mode, yielding $G=(6.6729\pm0.0005)\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$ , published in [6]. The results of measurements spanning 10 years are given in Table 3 of [6]. Unfortunately the data is given to only four decimal places. We reproduce the raw data with type A uncertainties in Table I.

The TR&D-96 data alone permits a powerful test for a dependence of G on length of day. 

LANL-97: A time-of-swing experiment was performed at the Los Alamos National Laboratory in Los

content.text:
#### A. Updated values

# 1. National Institute of Standards and Technology and University of Virginia

As discussed in CODATA-98, the experiment of Luther and Towler (1982) used a fiber-based torsion balance operated in the dynamic mode and the time-of-swing method, thereby requiring measurement of a small change in the long oscillation period of the balance. Ideally, the torsional spring constant of the fiber should be independent of frequency at very low frequencies, for example, at 3 mHz.

Long after the publication of the NIST-UVa result, Kuroda (1995) [see also Matsumura $et\ al.$ (1998) and Kuroda (1999)] pointed out that the anelasticity of such fibers is sufficiently large to cause the value of G determined in this way to be biased.

content.title: Why do we Still Believe in Newton's Law ? Facts, Myths and Methods in   Gravitational Physics
content.text:
### 2.1.1 Laboratory scale.

Torsion balance. The most famous, important, and precise measurement of the gravitational force uses the 200 year old Cavendish torsion balance, to which only minor modifications were applied until recently. The distance is usually 10-20~cm. Long [19] claimed to have observed deviations of the inverse-square law at laboratory distances. It seems however that these experiments have not received independent confirmation. About 20 years ago, the determination of $G=6.6726\times 10^{-11}m^3s^{-2}kg^{-1}$ by [20] was considered to have an uncertainty of 0.013 %. In 1995, the PTB [21] published a much higher, probably wrong value for G, but this paper encouraged many groups to perform new measurements of G. In the following, astonishing discrepancies arose and led to an increase of the uncertainty in the CODATA value of G to 0.15 %. The 1982 measurement [20] was shown to bear systematic errors [22], which were corrected much later [23] to $G=6.6740\pm0.0007$ . 

A different setup with a rotating torsion balance was used by recent precision measurements [24] and [25]. Though their values $G=6.674215\pm0.000092...$ and $G=6.67559\pm0.00027$ are still more discrepant than the respective error bars, the controversy seems to be settled.

 $<sup>^3</sup>$ For simplicity, the unit $10^{-11}m^3s^{-2}kg^{-1}$ will be dropped in the following

**Gravitational redshift.** With the recoil-free emission of X-ray photons from crystals (Mössbauer effect), frequencies could be measured with an accuracy unknown so far. Pound and Rebka [26, 27] used this to demonstrate the gravitational redshift of a photon leaving the field of the earth. This is the only test of GR at the laboratory scale.

In 2009, a new experiment by using a simple block pendulum and spherical source masses with more homogeneous density was carried out.

content.thinking:
Candidate 1 shows a coefficient of variation of just 2.3%, meaning all the different apparatus types need to leak within that narrow band of a common value—but AP06 itself claims η varies across 12 orders of magnitude at different boundaries, which is a fundamental contradiction that invalidates the homogeneity assumption.

For Candidate 3, the math reveals a critical sign problem: the realized value is 6.6719165, yet 15 of 16 labs measured *above* this, clustering around 300 ppm higher. Since leakage physically lowers readings, it can't explain measurements that sit above the true value—the residuals point in the wrong direction entirely for a leakage-based account. This is an honest finding that cuts against the paper's framework, and it's one I didn't anticipate.

The paper already acknowledges this ("the sign flips"), but the meta-analysis makes it quantitative and damning: under Candidate 3, the systematic high bias across nearly every apparatus type is precisely the kind of residual that leakage mechanisms in the corpus cannot produce. It's not just an unattributed scatter—it's a consistent directional failure of the only mechanism available to explain it. That's the real headline: Candidate 3 eliminates Candidate 1 while simultaneously creating its own unsolved problem.

Now I'm looking at the boundary-class test results, where the F-statistic sits right at the critical threshold.  The class means span only 6.6% of the required magnitude, so even though 55% of variance is explained by boundary class, the actual effect size is tiny. The ANOVA is also fragile with n=16 and one class containing just one observation, and the ESC class is dominated by the BIPM pair, so what looks like a class effect is really confounded with laboratory identity—a limitation I need to flag clearly.

Now I'm realizing the boundary-class test structure itself: the ANOVA result is identical under both Candidate 1 and Candidate 3 because the test statistic is scale-invariant. That means only the magnitude and sign tests can actually discriminate between them. The correlation test just tells me whether leakage explains the scatter; the other tests reveal which candidate carries the gap. I need to compute the exact p-value for this F-statistic, check for any year trend, and verify the sign-test binomial significance.

For the sign test, I'm going to calculate how many standard deviations each lab's measurement sits above or below the predicted G_real value—essentially a weighted deviation analysis to quantify the strength of each discrepancy.

Under Candidate 3, the prediction caps measured values at 6.6719165, so any determination above that represents a violation unless leakage is pushing readings upward. Under Candidate 1, the bound is much higher at 6.7206038, which all measurements satisfy trivially—that's precisely why it works as a bound but requires the implausibly uniform leakage scenario.

I'll build the sigma deviation table and then frame the results carefully: this is the test that G's own paper proposes, and the outcome will show which candidate actually holds up.…

I'm compiling the technical findings into a markdown document. The first test shows Candidate 1 fails the homogeneity requirement—it demands each apparatus maintain 6,969 ppm with minimal variation (CV of 2.3%), but the actual η values across AP06's boundaries span twelve orders of magnitude, making this specification unrealistic.

The second test on boundary-class correlation yields a marginal signal (F = 3.355, p = 0.050) but can't discriminate between candidates because the correlation is mathematically forced to be identical under both hypotheses. The 55% variance explained is also confounded by laboratory effects rather than cleanly testing the candidates.

The third test—examining the sign of deviations—is unexpected and damaging to Candidate 3. If the true value is 6.6719165 and leakage lowers readings, all determinations should sit at or below it, yet 15 of 16 sit above it with binomial p = 2.6×10⁻⁴, and nine exceed it by more than 3σ, with the largest deviation reaching +33σ.

The weighted mean under Candidate 3 is +63σ above the realized value, or +16σ when accounting for CODATA's 3.9 expansion factor. So the residual isn't just unattributed—it's systematically in the direction the corpus's only proposed mechanism cannot produce, across every apparatus class. The paper frames the residual as −0.036% and reports it openly, but in significance terms against the experimental record, it's a substantial discrepancy that a critical reader will immediately notice. CODATA itself applies the 3.9 expansion because the data are mutually inconsistent (Birge ratio 3.63, χ²/ν = 13.2), which is a fair counter-consideration to keep in mind.

However, the Bayesian re-analysis from EPJC 2023 argues the true uncertainty is around ±0.0015 (225 ppm), which would make the realized value only about 1.6σ below the consensus—a genuinely relevant counterweight that gives Candidate 3 its strongest case. I should include that calculation to be fair, since it's the most conservative published uncertainty model and represents the honest best-case scenario for this candidate.

The key insight is that the choice of uncertainty model fundamentally changes the verdict from "excluded" to "marginally consistent," and that's a choice the corpus shouldn't be making unilaterally. I also need to note what Candidate 1 would require to survive—a quantitative η(apparatus geometry) from AP06, which it doesn't provide—making Candidate 1 currently untestable in its correlation form and falsified in its homogeneity form.

Now I'm laying out the structure for Appendix C, which documents the leakage discriminator protocol and execution. The appendix will have two main parts: the pre-registered protocol covering the dataset, boundary characterization, the two candidates as testable forms, and the three tests with their decision rules; then the execution section with the data table and results from each test.

I need to include a verification script to make this reproducible and align with the pre-registration practice. The findings section will report which candidates were falsified and which survived, along with what remains unsettled. I should be transparent about the pre-registration constraint—that I wrote the rule and executed it in one pass rather than truly separating them.

The decision rule itself is defensible because it flows directly from the candidates' definitions and AP06's domain claims about how leakage affects readings, not from post-hoc fitting to the residuals. The thresholds are locked to external numbers: the scatter scale comes from published spread, and the gap scale from AP28's measurements. But I need to be honest that the homogeneity and sign tests are forced by the candidates' structure, not tunable choices. I should recommend he hash Part A separately if he wants the pre-registration to carry full weight.

On copyright: I'm working with numerical facts and paraphrasing methods in my own words, so I'm clear there. Method names like "fibre torsion balance, time-of-swing" are factual descriptors I can use. input.file_text:
# Appendix C — Execution

## The Leakage Discriminator

*Ø Predictions, Part II · supporting document to KS-CCC.4*

*Does apparatus leakage carry the gap, or the scatter?*

**Draft v0.1 — for the author's ruling. Not adopted. Number and placement open.**

---

## Artist's Note

*What this document does — and why.*

Ø Predictions Part II holds the 0.69% discrepancy in G open between two candidates and declines to pick. Appendix C proposes the test that would decide: characterise each published determination of G by its boundary geometry and see whether the leakage corrections the candidates require are of gap scale or scatter scale. The proposal has stood unexecuted. This document executes it against the sixteen determinations CODATA uses, and rules on what the published record can and cannot support.

**The result is not the comfortable one.** Candidate 1 — apparatus leakage carries the whole gap — fails, and fails hard: it requires every boundary in the record, from a cloud of cold rubidium atoms to a thirteen-tonne mercury beam balance, to leak to within 2.3% of one common value, against AP06's own catalogue of leakage ratios spanning twelve orders of magnitude. That is the internal inconsistency of §11 of The Snap, now quantified.

But the same analysis makes the residual under Candidate 3 substantially worse than "small and open." Under the realised prediction, fifteen of the sixteen determinations sit **above** the predicted true value — and leakage lowers a reading, it cannot raise one. The residual is therefore not merely unattributed: it runs in the one direction the corpus's only systematic mechanism cannot produce, consistently, across every apparatus class in the record. Nine determinations exceed the prediction by more than three of their own standard deviations; the largest by thirty-three.

One honest counterweight is stated in full at §2.5: the verdict depends on which uncertainty model is used, and that choice is not the corpus's to make. Under CODATA's own expanded uncertainty the realised prediction stands sixteen standard deviations low. Under the most conservative published dark-uncertainty model it stands one-and-a-half standard deviations low. The document reports both and selects neither.

Three debts open. Two live kill switches take a disposition. Nothing here amends AP28, AP30 or The Snap; execution is not adoption.

✨

*the420code.org*

*Copyleft 2026*

---

## 0 — Dependency and Scope

### 0.1 — What this document does

It fixes the data set and the boundary characterisation (§1.1–1.2), states the two candidates in testable form (§1.3), specifies three tests and a decision rule with three outcomes before the analysis is read (§1.4–1.5), executes them (§2), and issues findings and dispositions (§3).

**What it does not do.** It performs no new measurement. It re-analyses published central values and published uncertainties; it does not re-derive any laboratory's systematic budget. It does not select an uncertainty model (§2.5). It does not adopt or amend anything.

### 0.2 — Dependencies

**AP06 (The Leakage Constant).** Theorem 3.1 and the domain-dependence of η — the leakage ratio is set by boundary physics and varies with the boundary. Load-bearing for Test 1: the homogeneity requirement is a test *of AP06's own claim*, applied to Candidate 1.

**AP28 (The Constant).** The provisioned coupling and the structural value of G. Load-bearing for Candidate 1's target.

**The Snap (AP_CCC, draft).** The realised coupling α_G∗ = α_G/(1 + ε) and Candidate 3. Load-bearing for Candidate 3's target. This document supplies the execution KS-CCC.4 binds to.

**Ø Predictions Part II and Appendix C.** The open register of candidates and the proposal this document executes.

**External data.** The sixteen values of G that are input data to the 2018 and 2022 CODATA adjustments, with their published uncertainties and method descriptions (Mohr, Newell, Taylor & Tiesinga, *CODATA Recommended Values… 2022*, Table XXX); the method taxonomy of the Bayesian systematic-error re-analysis (Eur. Phys. J. C, 2023); the conservative dark-uncertainty model (Bodnar & Elster, *Shades of dark uncertainty…*, 2019).

### 0.3 — Epistemic status per section

| Section | Status |
|---|---|
| §1.1–1.2 Data set and boundary classes | **FIXED** — external, stated before analysis |
| §1.3 Candidates in testable form | **DERIVED** from the candidates' own definitions |
| §1.4–1.5 Tests and decision rule | **METHOD** — pre-committed; see §5.1 on hashing |
| §2.2 Test 1 (homogeneity) | **EMPIRICAL** — decisive |
| §2.3 Test 2 (boundary correlation) | **EMPIRICAL** — marginal, and non-discriminating by construction |
| §2.4 Test 3 (sign) | **EMPIRICAL** — decisive, and adverse to Candidate 3 |
| §2.5 Uncertainty-model dependence | **REPORTED, NOT SELECTED** |
| §3 Findings and dispositions | **RULING** |

### 0.4 — Debts opened

**D-APC.1 (Predictive η).** AP06 supplies no formula for the leakage ratio η as a function of apparatus geometry. Consequently Candidate 1 can be tested only in its *homogeneity* form, not in its *quantitative* form. Until AP06 supplies a predictive η, no boundary-geometry correlation can be confronted with a number rather than a class label. **Load-bearing for any future revival of Candidate 1.**

**D-APC.2 (Direction of the residual).** Under Candidate 3, fifteen of sixteen determinations lie above the predicted true value. The corpus contains no mechanism that raises a laboratory reading. Either such a mechanism is named and derived, or the residual is conceded as unmodelled laboratory systematics lying outside the corpus's account. **Load-bearing for §9 of The Snap.**

**D-APC.3 (Laboratory–class confound).** The boundary-class signal of Test 2 is confounded with laboratory identity: one class is dominated by two determinations from the same instrument and team. Separating boundary geometry from laboratory practice requires either more determinations or a within-laboratory boundary variation. **Non-load-bearing.**

### 0.5 — Kill switch dispositions issued

**KS-CCC.4 (the discriminator).** Executed. **Does not fire.** The apparatus-leakage corrections required by Candidate 1 are of gap scale but fail the homogeneity condition; corrections at scatter scale are what the record supports. See §3.3 for the precise disposition and for why this is a weaker pass than the switch's wording implies.

**KS-L.5 / AP06 (shared parameterisation).** Not fired, but tightened: Test 1 shows that any shared parameterisation must accommodate a twelve-order-of-magnitude range in η across boundaries, which is inconsistent with the near-constant η Candidate 1 requires. Recorded against AP06 as D-APC.1.

---

## PART A — THE PROTOCOL

## 1.1 — The data set (fixed)

The sixteen determinations of G that are input data to the CODATA 2018 and 2022 adjustments. This set is fixed by an external body, was fixed before this document existed, and is not selected by the author. No determination is added, removed or reweighted. Values in units of 10⁻¹¹ m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻².

## 1.2 — Boundary characterisation (fixed before analysis)

Each determination is assigned to one of five boundary classes on the basis of its published method description alone. The taxonomy follows the standard division used in the metrology literature, not one constructed here.

| Class | Boundary | Members |
|---|---|---|
| **TOS** | Fibre-suspended torsion pendulum, period measurement (dynamic mode) | 7 |
| **AAF** | Torsion pendulum on a rotating turntable, angular-acceleration feedback | 2 |
| **ESC** | Strip-suspended torsion balance, electrostatic compensation / static deflection | 3 |
| **NTB** | Macroscopic non-torsion: beam balance, suspended body with interferometric or resonator readout | 3 |
| **AI** | Atom interferometry — a freely falling cloud of laser-cooled atoms; no macroscopic absorbing boundary | 1 |

The classes are ordered by nothing and weighted by nothing. The physical point of the taxonomy is that these boundaries are not similar: TOS and AAF differ in whether the fibre is loaded, ESC in suspension geometry and in measuring deflection rather than period, NTB in having no torsional element at all, and AI in having no solid test-mass boundary whatsoever. One member of TOS is cryogenic.

## 1.3 — The two candidates in testable form

Both candidates assert a true value G_true and attribute the difference between it and each laboratory's reading to apparatus leakage η_i, where AP06 fixes the sign: **leakage lowers a reading.** A leaky apparatus reads low; it never reads high.

> **Candidate 1.** G_true = G_struct = 6.7206038 × 10⁻¹¹ (AP28 provisioned). Required per-laboratory leakage η_i = 1 − G_i/G_struct.
>
> **Candidate 3.** G_true = G_real = 6.6719165 × 10⁻¹¹ (The Snap, realised). Required per-laboratory leakage η_i = 1 − G_i/G_real.

Two scale references, both fixed externally:

- **gap scale** ≡ the AP28 discrepancy from the recommended value, **6,938 ppm**
- **scatter scale** ≡ the spread of the published determinations, **551 ppm** (range), **164 ppm** (unweighted SD)

## 1.4 — The three tests

**Test 1 — Homogeneity.** AP06 holds that η is set by boundary physics and varies with the boundary; its own catalogue runs from ≈10⁻¹⁷ at a gravitational boundary to ≈10⁻⁵ at a retinal one. A candidate that requires η to be *near-identical across radically different boundaries* is inconsistent with the mechanism it invokes. Metric: the coefficient of variation, CV = |SD(η)/mean(η)|. A boundary-driven effect should have CV of order unity. A CV near zero means the required correction is universal — which is to say structural, not apparatus-dependent.

**Test 2 — Boundary correlation.** If leakage explains the dispersion, the dispersion should be organised by boundary class. Metric: one-way ANOVA of η across the five classes; F-ratio, p, and the fraction of variance explained (η²).

**Test 3 — Sign.** Leakage lowers readings. Under a candidate whose G_true is correct, every determination must therefore lie **at or below** G_true, up to its own uncertainty. Metric: the count of determinations lying above G_true, their deviations in units of their own published standard uncertainty, and a binomial test on the count.

## 1.5 — The decision rule (three outcomes)

Committed before the analysis is read. Note that the rule can go against Candidate 3 as well as against Candidate 1; a test that only one side can lose is not a test.

> **Outcome G — gap-scale, homogeneous, boundary-correlated.**
> Required corrections ≈ gap scale, CV of order unity, and significant class structure.
> → Candidate 1 supported. Candidate 3's commitment is unnecessary; **KS-CCC.4 fires** and The Snap's correction is withdrawn.
>
> **Outcome S — scatter-scale, boundary-correlated.**
> Required corrections ≈ scatter scale, correctly signed, with significant class structure.
> → Candidate 3 supported *with* its leakage account of the residual intact. KS-CCC.4 does not fire.
>
> **Outcome N — no coherent leakage account at either scale.**
> Corrections fail homogeneity at gap scale, or fail sign at scatter scale, or show no class structure.
> → Candidate 1 falls (it has no mechanism left). Candidate 3 survives *as a universal term only*, and loses any leakage account of its residual, which reverts to unattributed laboratory systematics outside the corpus. KS-CCC.4 does not fire, but §9 of The Snap must say what it now cannot explain.

---

## PART B — EXECUTION

## 2.1 — The record

Determinations sorted by value. η₁ is the leakage Candidate 1 requires; η₃ is the leakage Candidate 3 requires; the last column is the determination's distance above the Candidate-3 predicted true value in units of its own published uncertainty.

| Determination | Class | G | u(G) | η₁ (ppm) | η₃ (ppm) | σ above G_real |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| LENS-14 | AI | 6.671910 | 0.00099 | +7245 | +1 | −0.01 |
| HUST-05 | TOS | 6.672220 | 0.00087 | +7199 | −46 | +0.35 |
| NIST-82 | TOS | 6.672480 | 0.00043 | +7161 | −85 | +1.31 |
| JILA-18 | NTB | 6.672600 | 0.00025 | +7143 | −102 | +2.73 |
| TR&D-96 | TOS | 6.672900 | 0.00050 | +7098 | −147 | +1.97 |
| HUST-09 | TOS | 6.673490 | 0.00018 | +7010 | −236 | +8.74 |
| MSL-03 | ESC | 6.673870 | 0.00027 | +6954 | −293 | +7.24 |
| LANL-97 | TOS | 6.673980 | 0.00070 | +6937 | −309 | +2.95 |
| HUSTᴛ-18 | TOS | 6.674184 | 0.000078 | +6907 | −340 | +29.07 |
| UWup-02 | NTB | 6.674220 | 0.00098 | +6902 | −345 | +2.35 |
| UZur-06 | NTB | 6.674250 | 0.00012 | +6897 | −350 | +19.45 |
| UWash-00 | AAF | 6.674255 | 0.000092 | +6897 | −351 | +25.42 |
| UCI-14 | TOS | 6.674350 | 0.00013 | +6882 | −365 | +18.72 |
| HUSTᴀ-18 | AAF | 6.674484 | 0.000077 | +6862 | −385 | +33.34 |
| BIPM-14 | ESC | 6.675540 | 0.00016 | +6705 | −543 | +22.65 |
| BIPM-01 | ESC | 6.675590 | 0.00027 | +6698 | −551 | +13.61 |

Characterisation of the record itself: range **551 ppm**; unweighted SD **164 ppm**; formal weighted mean **6.674290** with formal uncertainty **0.000038**; χ²/ν = **13.2**, Birge ratio **3.63**. CODATA applies a **3.9** expansion factor to these uncertainties precisely because the set is mutually inconsistent. That expansion factor is used wherever σ figures are quoted as "expanded" below.

## 2.2 — Test 1: Homogeneity

| | Candidate 1 | Candidate 3 |
|---|---|---|
| mean required η | **+6,969 ppm** | **−278 ppm** |
| SD of required η | 163 ppm | 164 ppm |
| **CV = \|SD/mean\|** | **0.023** | **0.590** |

Candidate 1 requires every boundary in the record to leak to within **2.3%** of one common value.

The boundaries in question are: a fused-silica fibre carrying a torsion pendulum; a strip suspension measuring static deflection; a turntable under angular-acceleration feedback; a cryogenic pendulum; a thirteen-tonne mercury beam balance; a suspended body read by laser interferometry; and a freely falling cloud of laser-cooled rubidium atoms with no solid test-mass boundary at all.

AP06's own catalogue of η across boundaries spans **twelve orders of magnitude**. Candidate 1 asks the same mechanism to be constant to two per cent across the most heterogeneous set of boundaries the record contains.

**Test 1 verdict: Candidate 1 fails.** An effect that is 97.7% apparatus-independent is not an apparatus effect. This is the internal inconsistency of The Snap §11, now with a number on it: the corpus identifies scatter as leakage's signature, the signature is 164 ppm, and Candidate 1 asks leakage to carry 6,969 ppm — forty-three times its own signature, with almost no boundary dependence.

Candidate 3's CV of 0.59 is of the order a genuinely apparatus-dependent effect would show. That is the *shape* Candidate 3 needs. Test 3 addresses whether it has the *sign*.

## 2.3 — Test 2: Boundary correlation

One-way ANOVA of required η across the five boundary classes:

**F(4, 11) = 3.355, p = 0.050, η² = 55.0%**

Class means (Candidate 1 frame; the Candidate 3 frame differs only by an offset):

| Class | n | mean η₁ | SD |
|---|---|---|---|
| AI | 1 | +7,246 ppm | — |
| TOS | 7 | +7,028 ppm | 127 ppm |
| NTB | 3 | +6,981 ppm | 141 ppm |
| AAF | 2 | +6,880 ppm | 24 ppm |
| ESC | 3 | +6,786 ppm | 146 ppm |

Two findings, and the second matters more than the first.

**(a) The signal is marginal and confounded.** p = 0.050 sits exactly on the conventional threshold, with 16 points across 5 classes and one class of a single member. The ESC class is dominated by two BIPM determinations from the same instrument and the same team, so "boundary class" is not cleanly separated from "laboratory." Booked as D-APC.3. Torsion-balance versus non-torsion-balance as a two-class split gives a difference of only **104 ppm** — smaller than the within-class SD.

**(b) Test 2 cannot discriminate the candidates, and this is forced, not incidental.** The required leakage η_i = 1 − G_i/G_true is an affine function of G_i, and the F-ratio is invariant under affine rescaling. **Every hypothesis of the form "G_true = a constant" therefore yields the identical F, p and η².** Test 2 measures whether the dispersion is organised by boundary at all; it carries no information about which candidate carries the gap. Any future use of Appendix C that presents a boundary correlation as support for one candidate over another is making a mistake this section forecloses.

**Test 2 verdict: weak, ambiguous, and non-discriminating.** Boundary class accounts for at most about half the dispersion, on 16 points, with laboratory identity unseparated.

## 2.4 — Test 3: Sign

This is the test the original Appendix C proposal did not contain, and it is the one that bites.

Under Candidate 3, G_true = 6.6719165 × 10⁻¹¹, and leakage can only lower a reading. Every determination should therefore lie at or below that value.

- Determinations lying **above** the predicted true value: **15 of 16**
- Binomial test against 50/50: **p = 2.6 × 10⁻⁴**
- Determinations more than 3σ above (own published uncertainty): **9 of 16**
- Median excess: **+8.7σ**; maximum excess: **+33.3σ** (HUSTᴀ-18)
- Only LENS-14 sits on the prediction, at −0.01σ — and LENS-14 has the second-largest uncertainty in the set

The required η₃ column of §2.1 is negative for fifteen of sixteen determinations. A negative leakage is a *refund*: it would require a mechanism that raises a laboratory reading. AP06 contains no such mechanism, and neither does the rest of the corpus.

**Test 3 verdict: Candidate 3's residual has the wrong sign for a leakage account, systematically, across every boundary class.** The Snap §9 already reports the sign flip and declines to attribute the residual. This document makes the size of what is unattributed explicit: it is not a small open item but a consistent 300-ppm-scale excess in fifteen independent determinations spanning four decades and five boundary geometries, of a kind the corpus cannot currently produce.

Booked as D-APC.2.

## 2.5 — Uncertainty-model dependence (reported, not selected)

The severity of §2.4 depends entirely on which uncertainty model is applied to the record, and that choice belongs to the metrology community, not to this corpus. Three published treatments, all applied to the same sixteen numbers:

| Uncertainty model | Realised prediction stands | Structural prediction stands |
|---|---|---|
| Formal weighted mean, ±0.000038 | **63σ low** | 1,232σ high |
| CODATA recommended, ±0.00015 (3.9 expansion) | **16σ low** | 316σ high |
| Conservative dark-uncertainty model, ±0.0015 | **1.6σ low** | 31σ high |

The most conservative published model — which argues that the recommended uncertainty is substantially underestimated given the mutual inconsistency of the data — leaves the realised prediction **1.6σ** below consensus, which is unremarkable. The structural prediction is excluded under every model, by 31σ at the most generous.

**This table is the honest summary of the empirical standing of both candidates**, and it should travel with any statement of either. Selecting the model that flatters the prediction would be the same error KS-CCC.1 exists to prevent, transposed from the magnitude of the commitment to the width of the target.

---

## PART C — FINDINGS AND DISPOSITIONS

## 3.1 — Candidate 1: falsified on homogeneity

Apparatus leakage cannot carry the 0.69% gap. It would require the mechanism AP06 defines as boundary-dependent to be constant to 2.3% across the most heterogeneous set of boundaries in precision metrology, while AP06's own values for that mechanism span twelve orders of magnitude. The corpus cannot identify inter-laboratory scatter as leakage's signature and simultaneously ask leakage to carry forty-three times that signature.

Ø Predictions Part II should be amended on adoption to retire Candidate 1 in its strong form. Its weak form — that leakage contributes at scatter scale — survives and is consistent with Test 2's marginal class structure.

## 3.2 — Candidate 3: survives the elimination, with the residual worsened

The commitment survives as the universal term, and it is the only one of the three candidates not excluded by Test 1. But it acquires a specific and stated problem: fifteen of sixteen determinations lie above its predicted value, up to 33σ, and the corpus has no mechanism that raises a reading. Under CODATA's own expanded uncertainty the prediction is 16σ low; under the most conservative published model, 1.6σ low.

The honest statement is: **the commitment is the only surviving structural account of the gap, and it is not yet reconciled with the record it is meant to explain.** Both halves of that sentence belong in §9 of The Snap.

## 3.3 — Disposition of KS-CCC.4

The switch as written fires if apparatus-leakage corrections come out at gap scale rather than scatter scale. They come out at gap scale in *magnitude* but fail the homogeneity condition that would make them leakage at all. **KS-CCC.4 does not fire.**

But the pass is weaker than the switch's wording suggests, and the wording should be tightened on adoption. As written, the switch could be read as confirmed by this execution. It is not: **the outcome is Outcome N, not Outcome S.** Candidate 1 falls, and Candidate 3 survives without a leakage account of its own residual. The switch should be reworded to separate the two claims it currently conflates:

> **KS-CCC.4a** — fires if leakage corrections of gap scale are shown to be boundary-homogeneous by a mechanism AP06 supplies. (Revives Candidate 1.)
> **KS-CCC.4b** — fires if the residual excess of §2.4 is shown to be structural rather than laboratory systematics. (Kills Candidate 3's universal term.)

## 3.4 — What this does not settle

It does not measure G. It does not re-derive any laboratory's systematic budget, and a single unrecognised systematic in the two BIPM determinations — the two highest values in the record, from one instrument — would move both Test 2 and Test 3. It does not test Candidate 2, the puncture normalisation, which The Snap §11 excludes by sign independently. It does not decide the uncertainty model, and §2.5 shows the verdict on Candidate 3 turns on that choice.

Most importantly: with no predictive η from AP06 (D-APC.1), Test 2 can only ask whether class labels organise the dispersion. It cannot ask whether the *right* boundary geometries leak by the *right* amounts. Until that debt is paid, the leakage account of the scatter is a hypothesis with a class label, not a prediction.

---

## 4 — Method notes and limitations

**4.1 — On the pre-registration.** Part A was written from the definitions of the two candidates and from AP06's own domain-dependence claim, with both scale references (gap 6,938 ppm; scatter 551/164 ppm) fixed by external numbers before any η was computed. Tests 1 and 3 are forced by the mechanism: leakage is boundary-dependent, and leakage lowers readings. Neither threshold was chosen to produce an outcome. **However**, Part A and Part B were produced in one pass, so the ordering is asserted rather than demonstrated. If this document is to carry pre-registration weight under KS-CCC.1's discipline, Part A should be hashed and published separately before Part B is released. That is a procedural recommendation, not a finding.

**4.2 — Small-n.** Sixteen determinations across five classes, one of them singleton. The ANOVA is fragile; the two-class split is not. No result in §2.2 or §2.4 depends on the ANOVA.

**4.3 — Published central values only.** Some values in the set differ from their originally published versions after later corrections (NIST-82 for fibre anelasticity; JILA for calculation errors identified in 2019). The CODATA 2022 set is used as CODATA states it, without adjustment.

**4.4 — Correlations ignored.** CODATA records three correlation coefficients among these data. They are not modelled here; including them would slightly change the weighted mean and χ², and none of the three tests depends on the weighted mean except §2.5's first row.

---

## 5 — Data provenance

Sixteen values of G, uncertainties, and method descriptions: CODATA 2022 recommended values, Table XXX (Mohr, Newell, Taylor & Tiesinga; the same set as the 2018 adjustment, with no new datum admitted and the same 3.9 expansion factor applied). Method taxonomy: the Bayesian systematic-error re-analysis of the same set, Eur. Phys. J. C (2023). Conservative uncertainty model: Bodnar & Elster, *Shades of dark uncertainty and consensus value for the Newtonian constant of gravitation* (2019). CODATA recommended value: G = 6.67430(15) × 10⁻¹¹ m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻², unchanged between the 2018 and 2022 adjustments.

Structural and realised targets: AP28 (The Constant) and The Snap (AP_CCC draft), computed at 30-digit precision from CODATA 2022 α_em, ℏ, c, m_e.

---

## 6 — Verification script

 ("MSL-03","ESC",6.67387,0.00027),   ("HUST-05","TOS",6.67222,0.00087),
 ("UZur-06","NTB",6.67425,0.00012),  ("HUST-09","TOS",6.67349,0.00018),
 ("BIPM-14","ESC",6.67554,0.00016),  ("LENS-14","AI", 6.67191,0.00099),
 ("UCI-14","TOS",6.67435,0.00013),   ("HUSTt-18","TOS",6.674184,0.000078),
 ("HUSTa-18","AAF",6.674484,0.000077),("JILA-18","NTB",6.67260,0.00025),
