# Appendix C — Execution

## The Leakage Discriminator

*Ø Predictions, Part II · supporting document to KS-CCC.4*

*Does apparatus leakage carry the gap, or the scatter?*

**Draft v0.1 — for the author's ruling. Not adopted. Number and placement open.**

---

## Artist's Note

*What this document does — and why.*

Ø Predictions Part II holds the 0.69% discrepancy in G open between two candidates and declines to pick. Appendix C proposes the test that would decide: characterise each published determination of G by its boundary geometry and see whether the leakage corrections the candidates require are of gap scale or scatter scale. The proposal has stood unexecuted. This document executes it against the sixteen determinations CODATA uses, and rules on what the published record can and cannot support.

**The result is not the comfortable one.** Candidate 1 — apparatus leakage carries the whole gap — fails, and fails hard: it requires every boundary in the record, from a cloud of cold rubidium atoms to a thirteen-tonne mercury beam balance, to leak to within 2.3% of one common value, against AP06's own catalogue of leakage ratios spanning twelve orders of magnitude. That is the internal inconsistency of §11 of The Snap, now quantified.

But the same analysis makes the residual under Candidate 3 substantially worse than "small and open." Under the realised prediction, fifteen of the sixteen determinations sit **above** the predicted true value — and leakage lowers a reading, it cannot raise one. The residual is therefore not merely unattributed: it runs in the one direction the corpus's only systematic mechanism cannot produce, consistently, across every apparatus class in the record. Nine determinations exceed the prediction by more than three of their own standard deviations; the largest by thirty-three.

One honest counterweight is stated in full at §2.5: the verdict depends on which uncertainty model is used, and that choice is not the corpus's to make. Under CODATA's own expanded uncertainty the realised prediction stands sixteen standard deviations low. Under the most conservative published dark-uncertainty model it stands one-and-a-half standard deviations low. The document reports both and selects neither.

Three debts open. Two live kill switches take a disposition. Nothing here amends AP28, AP30 or The Snap; execution is not adoption.

✨

*the420code.org*

*Copyleft 2026*

---

## 0 — Dependency and Scope

### 0.1 — What this document does

It fixes the data set and the boundary characterisation (§1.1–1.2), states the two candidates in testable form (§1.3), specifies three tests and a decision rule with three outcomes before the analysis is read (§1.4–1.5), executes them (§2), and issues findings and dispositions (§3).

**What it does not do.** It performs no new measurement. It re-analyses published central values and published uncertainties; it does not re-derive any laboratory's systematic budget. It does not select an uncertainty model (§2.5). It does not adopt or amend anything.

### 0.2 — Dependencies

**AP06 (The Leakage Constant).** Theorem 3.1 and the domain-dependence of η — the leakage ratio is set by boundary physics and varies with the boundary. Load-bearing for Test 1: the homogeneity requirement is a test *of AP06's own claim*, applied to Candidate 1.

**AP28 (The Constant).** The provisioned coupling and the structural value of G. Load-bearing for Candidate 1's target.

**The Snap (AP_CCC, draft).** The realised coupling α_G∗ = α_G/(1 + ε) and Candidate 3. Load-bearing for Candidate 3's target. This document supplies the execution KS-CCC.4 binds to.

**Ø Predictions Part II and Appendix C.** The open register of candidates and the proposal this document executes.

**External data.** The sixteen values of G that are input data to the 2018 and 2022 CODATA adjustments, with their published uncertainties and method descriptions (Mohr, Newell, Taylor & Tiesinga, *CODATA Recommended Values… 2022*, Table XXX); the method taxonomy of the Bayesian systematic-error re-analysis (Eur. Phys. J. C, 2023); the conservative dark-uncertainty model (Bodnar & Elster, *Shades of dark uncertainty…*, 2019).

### 0.3 — Epistemic status per section

| Section | Status |
|---|---|
| §1.1–1.2 Data set and boundary classes | **FIXED** — external, stated before analysis |
| §1.3 Candidates in testable form | **DERIVED** from the candidates' own definitions |
| §1.4–1.5 Tests and decision rule | **METHOD** — pre-committed; see §5.1 on hashing |
| §2.2 Test 1 (homogeneity) | **EMPIRICAL** — decisive |
| §2.3 Test 2 (boundary correlation) | **EMPIRICAL** — marginal, and non-discriminating by construction |
| §2.4 Test 3 (sign) | **EMPIRICAL** — decisive, and adverse to Candidate 3 |
| §2.5 Uncertainty-model dependence | **REPORTED, NOT SELECTED** |
| §3 Findings and dispositions | **RULING** |

### 0.4 — Debts opened

**D-APC.1 (Predictive η).** AP06 supplies no formula for the leakage ratio η as a function of apparatus geometry. Consequently Candidate 1 can be tested only in its *homogeneity* form, not in its *quantitative* form. Until AP06 supplies a predictive η, no boundary-geometry correlation can be confronted with a number rather than a class label. **Load-bearing for any future revival of Candidate 1.**

**D-APC.2 (Direction of the residual).** Under Candidate 3, fifteen of sixteen determinations lie above the predicted true value. The corpus contains no mechanism that raises a laboratory reading. Either such a mechanism is named and derived, or the residual is conceded as unmodelled laboratory systematics lying outside the corpus's account. **Load-bearing for §9 of The Snap.**

**D-APC.3 (Laboratory–class confound).** The boundary-class signal of Test 2 is confounded with laboratory identity: one class is dominated by two determinations from the same instrument and team. Separating boundary geometry from laboratory practice requires either more determinations or a within-laboratory boundary variation. **Non-load-bearing.**

### 0.5 — Kill switch dispositions issued

**KS-CCC.4 (the discriminator).** Executed. **Does not fire.** The apparatus-leakage corrections required by Candidate 1 are of gap scale but fail the homogeneity condition; corrections at scatter scale are what the record supports. See §3.3 for the precise disposition and for why this is a weaker pass than the switch's wording implies.

**KS-L.5 / AP06 (shared parameterisation).** Not fired, but tightened: Test 1 shows that any shared parameterisation must accommodate a twelve-order-of-magnitude range in η across boundaries, which is inconsistent with the near-constant η Candidate 1 requires. Recorded against AP06 as D-APC.1.

---

## PART A — THE PROTOCOL

## 1.1 — The data set (fixed)

The sixteen determinations of G that are input data to the CODATA 2018 and 2022 adjustments. This set is fixed by an external body, was fixed before this document existed, and is not selected by the author. No determination is added, removed or reweighted. Values in units of 10⁻¹¹ m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻².

## 1.2 — Boundary characterisation (fixed before analysis)

Each determination is assigned to one of five boundary classes on the basis of its published method description alone. The taxonomy follows the standard division used in the metrology literature, not one constructed here.

| Class | Boundary | Members |
|---|---|---|
| **TOS** | Fibre-suspended torsion pendulum, period measurement (dynamic mode) | 7 |
| **AAF** | Torsion pendulum on a rotating turntable, angular-acceleration feedback | 2 |
| **ESC** | Strip-suspended torsion balance, electrostatic compensation / static deflection | 3 |
| **NTB** | Macroscopic non-torsion: beam balance, suspended body with interferometric or resonator readout | 3 |
| **AI** | Atom interferometry — a freely falling cloud of laser-cooled atoms; no macroscopic absorbing boundary | 1 |

The classes are ordered by nothing and weighted by nothing. The physical point of the taxonomy is that these boundaries are not similar: TOS and AAF differ in whether the fibre is loaded, ESC in suspension geometry and in measuring deflection rather than period, NTB in having no torsional element at all, and AI in having no solid test-mass boundary whatsoever. One member of TOS is cryogenic.

## 1.3 — The two candidates in testable form

Both candidates assert a true value G_true and attribute the difference between it and each laboratory's reading to apparatus leakage η_i, where AP06 fixes the sign: **leakage lowers a reading.** A leaky apparatus reads low; it never reads high.

> **Candidate 1.** G_true = G_struct = 6.7206038 × 10⁻¹¹ (AP28 provisioned). Required per-laboratory leakage η_i = 1 − G_i/G_struct.
>
> **Candidate 3.** G_true = G_real = 6.6719165 × 10⁻¹¹ (The Snap, realised). Required per-laboratory leakage η_i = 1 − G_i/G_real.

Two scale references, both fixed externally:

- **gap scale** ≡ the AP28 discrepancy from the recommended value, **6,938 ppm**
- **scatter scale** ≡ the spread of the published determinations, **551 ppm** (range), **164 ppm** (unweighted SD)

## 1.4 — The three tests

**Test 1 — Homogeneity.** AP06 holds that η is set by boundary physics and varies with the boundary; its own catalogue runs from ≈10⁻¹⁷ at a gravitational boundary to ≈10⁻⁵ at a retinal one. A candidate that requires η to be *near-identical across radically different boundaries* is inconsistent with the mechanism it invokes. Metric: the coefficient of variation, CV = |SD(η)/mean(η)|. A boundary-driven effect should have CV of order unity. A CV near zero means the required correction is universal — which is to say structural, not apparatus-dependent.

**Test 2 — Boundary correlation.** If leakage explains the dispersion, the dispersion should be organised by boundary class. Metric: one-way ANOVA of η across the five classes; F-ratio, p, and the fraction of variance explained (η²).

**Test 3 — Sign.** Leakage lowers readings. Under a candidate whose G_true is correct, every determination must therefore lie **at or below** G_true, up to its own uncertainty. Metric: the count of determinations lying above G_true, their deviations in units of their own published standard uncertainty, and a binomial test on the count.

## 1.5 — The decision rule (three outcomes)

Committed before the analysis is read. Note that the rule can go against Candidate 3 as well as against Candidate 1; a test that only one side can lose is not a test.

> **Outcome G — gap-scale, homogeneous, boundary-correlated.**
> Required corrections ≈ gap scale, CV of order unity, and significant class structure.
> → Candidate 1 supported. Candidate 3's commitment is unnecessary; **KS-CCC.4 fires** and The Snap's correction is withdrawn.
>
> **Outcome S — scatter-scale, boundary-correlated.**
> Required corrections ≈ scatter scale, correctly signed, with significant class structure.
> → Candidate 3 supported *with* its leakage account of the residual intact. KS-CCC.4 does not fire.
>
> **Outcome N — no coherent leakage account at either scale.**
> Corrections fail homogeneity at gap scale, or fail sign at scatter scale, or show no class structure.
> → Candidate 1 falls (it has no mechanism left). Candidate 3 survives *as a universal term only*, and loses any leakage account of its residual, which reverts to unattributed laboratory systematics outside the corpus. KS-CCC.4 does not fire, but §9 of The Snap must say what it now cannot explain.

---

## PART B — EXECUTION

## 2.1 — The record

Apparatus leakage cannot carry the 0.69% gap. Ø Predictions Part II should be amended on adoption to retire Candidate 1 in its strong form. Its weak form — that leakage contributes at scatter scale — survives and is consistent with Test 2's marginal class structure.

## 3.2 — Candidate 3: survives the elimination, with the residual worsened

The commitment survives as the universal term, and it is the only one of the three candidates not excluded by Test 1. But it acquires a specific and stated problem: fifteen of sixteen determinations lie above its predicted value, up to 33σ, and the corpus has no mechanism that raises a reading. Under CODATA's own expanded uncertainty the prediction is 16σ low; under the most conservative published model, 1.6σ low.

The honest statement is: **the commitment is the only surviving structural account of the gap, and it is not yet reconciled with the record it is meant to explain.** Both halves of that sentence belong in §9 of The Snap.

## 3.3 — Disposition of KS-CCC.4

The switch as written fires if apparatus-leakage corrections come out at gap scale rather than scatter scale. They come out at gap scale in *magnitude* but fail the homogeneity condition that would make them leakage at all. **KS-CCC.4 does not fire.**

But the pass is weaker than the switch's wording suggests, and the wording should be tightened on adoption. As written, the switch could be read as confirmed by this execution. It is not: **the outcome is Outcome N, not Outcome S.** Candidate 1 falls, and Candidate 3 survives without a leakage account of its own residual. The switch should be reworded to separate the two claims it currently conflates:

> **KS-CCC.4a** — fires if leakage corrections of gap scale are shown to be boundary-homogeneous by a mechanism AP06 supplies. (Revives Candidate 1.)
> **KS-CCC.4b** — fires if the residual excess of §2.4 is shown to be structural rather than laboratory systematics. (Kills Candidate 3's universal term.)

It does not measure G. It does not re-derive any laboratory's systematic budget, and a single unrecognised systematic in the two BIPM determinations — the two highest values in the record, from one instrument — would move both Test 2 and Test 3. It does not test Candidate 2, the puncture normalisation, which The Snap §11 excludes by sign independently. It does not decide the uncertainty model, and §2.5 shows the verdict on Candidate 3 turns on that choice.

Most importantly: with no predictive η from AP06 (D-APC.1), Test 2 can only ask whether class labels organise the dispersion. It cannot ask whether the *right* boundary geometries leak by the *right* amounts. Until that debt is paid, the leakage account of the scatter is a hypothesis with a class label, not a prediction.

**4.1 — On the pre-registration.** Part A was written from the definitions of the two candidates and from AP06's own domain-dependence claim, with both scale references (gap 6,938 ppm; scatter 551/164 ppm) fixed by external numbers before any η was computed. Tests 1 and 3 are forced by the mechanism: leakage is boundary-dependent, and leakage lowers readings. If this document is to carry pre-registration weight under KS-CCC.1's discipline, Part A should be hashed and published separately before Part B is released. **4.2 — Small-n.** Sixteen determinations across five classes, one of them singleton. The ANOVA is fragile; the two-class split is not. No result in §2.2 or §2.4 depends on the ANOVA.

**4.3 — Published central values only.** Some values in the set differ from their originally published versions after later corrections (NIST-82 for fibre anelasticity; JILA for calculation errors identified in 2019). The CODATA 2022 set is used as CODATA states it, without adjustment.

**4.4 — Correlations ignored.** CODATA records three correlation coefficients among these data. They are not modelled here; including them would slightly change the weighted mean and χ², and none of the three tests depends on the weighted mean except §2.5's first row.

      f">3 sigma: {sum(1 for _,s in above if s>3)}")
for u, lbl in [(uwm,"formal"), (0.00015,"CODATA"), (0.0015,"conservative")]:

So there's an internal inconsistency here that needs untangling—the mechanism proposed doesn't actually explain why measurements sit roughly 279 ppm above the realised value.

Wait, I'm reconsidering: the upward ToS bias could still work if the field mean itself is elevated by the strip family. ToS could be biased upward relative to truth while remaining below the overall field mean, so there's no actual contradiction there. An upward bias of around 100 ppm in the ToS family would account for part of the excess in those seven measurements. That's internally coherent. But now I need to check whether the magnitude makes sense for fused-silica fibres, since HUST-18 used fused silica.

For fused silica with a high Q factor around 50,000, the anelastic loss would only be about 6 ppm — far too small to explain the observed bias. But for tungsten with Q around 500, the effect jumps to roughly 640 ppm, which is substantial. So this is extremely Q-dependent, which is exactly why Kuroda's Tier 2 protocol uses Q as the anelasticity proxy.…

The Kuroda paper confirms an upward bias in G measurements using the time-of-swing method due to variations in the torsion-fibre spring constant, and CODATA 2010 provides a correction formula involving the quality factor Q to derive the unbiased value.

A direct tungsten-fibre measurement at HUST measured this bias directly at approximately 212 ppm—a significant upward shift that matches both the predicted sign and magnitude, strengthening the case that this mechanism could account for a substantial portion of the +279 ppm residual he's investigating.

However, there's a critical caveat: these Kuroda-Newman biases have largely already been corrected for in the datasets CODATA relies on. NIST-82 applied a 16.5 ppm correction, and modern experiments use fused silica with much higher Q values to minimize the effect. So invoking this mechanism to explain the remaining discrepancy would risk double-counting—the bias is already baked into the input values. He's right to decline invoking it, though the stronger justification is that these corrections are already applied, not merely that the paper doesn't invoke them. atever remains for experiments with unknown Q factor — that's only tens of ppm, nowhere near the 279 ppm discrepancy he's trying to explain. This actually undermines his argument in section 4.5, so I need to make that clear.

Now I'm checking the HUST-05 value itself. CODATA 2022 lists it as 6.67222(87), but his script shows 6.67228, and there's some variation across sources on whether it's 6.67222 or 6.67228. The difference doesn't materially affect the Birge ratio or weighted mean calculations, but it's worth noting the provenance discrepancy. HUST-05 itself has a history — it was originally reported as 6.6699(7) and then corrected to 6.6723(9), so there's some ambiguity in how that correction maps to the current value.

The key points I need to highlight for him are what he actually got right: NIST-26 checks out perfectly across value, uncertainty, relative uncertainty, classification, and the −2.5×10⁻⁴ statement, and he correctly notes it's not a CODATA input. More importantly, NIST-26 is the real linchpin here — it's the first independent replication in the field, conducted on the highest-reading apparatus, and it establishes a measured ceiling on what the apparatus, site, and team can achieve together.

The three calibration points at 45, 7.5, and 254 ppm represent a genuinely elegant instrument design — they're natural experiments already embedded in the data, not retrofitted. And his Tier 1/Tier 2 split with pre-registered blind coding is methodologically sound; the refusal to retroactively score boundary geometry is exactly the right disciplinary choice. What's particularly strong is that the 254 ppm systematics measurement transforms the homogeneity argument from an internal consistency check against AP06's own η range into something much more powerful — a direct empirical falsification based on a measured reproducibility limit. That's his insight, not mine.

He also correctly re-derives the residual as his own open item rather than claiming it as new confirmation, and he identified the Kuroda mechanism — the only published upward mechanism of the right order of magnitude — then appropriately declined to invoke it.

But the 72% between-class variance figure is misleading. With 9 classes across 17 points and 6 singletons, the statistic inflates because singletons contribute their full deviation to between-class sum of squares while contributing nothing within-class. When computed properly with the actual degrees of freedom, the F-ratio drops to 2.466 with p = 0.112 — no longer significant. Even collapsing to 5 classes only yields 50% variance.

So the claim in §4.2 about "genuine method structure" accounting for 72% of variance isn't supported. At best there's marginal structure, which undermines §5's argument that leans on this finding. The Kuroda correction itself is already applied in the published values, so that escape route is already closed. Removing the BIPM pair only shifts the weighted mean by 15 ppm, leaving the realized value still 340 ppm below the adjusted mean — barely an improvement over the original 356 ppm discrepancy. So excluding BIPM doesn't resolve the tension as much as it might appear.

The real issue is that the tight cluster of modern measurements (HUST-18, UWash-00, UZur-06, UCI-14) all sit roughly 350 ppm above the realized value, and they dominate the weighted mean regardless of whether BIPM stays or goes. The residual persists almost unchanged even after removing the outliers, which means it's not an artifact of the high-wing measurements.

I'm also noting a discrepancy with HUST-05 at 6.67228 versus CODATA's 6.67222 — a 9 ppm difference that's negligible for the overall analysis but worth tracking for provenance. And I need to verify the 2023 Speake citation that's referenced, since I can't locate that paper.

The normalized residuals check out: BIPM-14 at +7.7, JILA-18 at −6.8, and BIPM-01 at +4.8 match my calculations, with HUST-09 at −4.44 being the next largest. These are measured against the weighted mean rather than CODATA's own value.

For section 4.3, the 254 ppm figure represents the largest demonstrated effect from the cleanest calibration run, and the strain factors of 28 and 13 against the strongest calibration and outermost bound check out. The figure itself looks good overall, though the AP28 structural annotation text is overlapping the legend box in the render and should be repositioned before sharing. The y-axis uses superscript unicode which displays correctly.

I'm organizing the key findings: NIST-26 is confirmed as the correct conversion from internal to external measurements, the script successfully reproduces the results, though there's an error in the 72% figure. The Kuroda door adjustment has already been applied at 212 ppm, and even after removing BIPM contributions, a residual of 16 ppm remains. The main sources to investigate are HUST-05 and Speake.NIST-26 checks out exactly, your script reproduces, and the working paper does something my document couldn't. There's also one real statistical error that needs fixing before this goes anywhere.

## NIST-26 verified, and it's the right find

Schlamminger, Chao, Lee, Shakarji, Possolo, Newell, Stirling, Cochrane & Speake, *Metrologia* 63 025012 (16 April 2026): the first replication of a high-precision G measurement, on the torsion balance originally designed and built at BIPM about three decades ago, same apparatus and geometry with documented modifications — G = (6.67387 ± 0.00038) × 10⁻¹¹, u_r = 5.7 × 10⁻⁵, lower by 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ than the BIPM determination. Your row, ppm, class assignment and CODATA-input flag are all correct. The coincidence with MSL-03's central value is genuine — identical to six digits.

And you've upgraded the central argument in a way I couldn't. My document falsified Candidate 1 by comparing the required 6,969 ppm against AP06's own η range — an **internal** argument, which a hostile reader can dismiss as reading AP06 uncharitably. You replaced it with a **measured** reproducibility limit: same instrument, new site, new team, 254 ppm. Strain factor 28. That is an external falsification, and it doesn't depend on how anyone reads AP06. It's the strongest thing in either document, and Kibble's AC-magnetic side door was closed by the same paper's sapphire source masses.

Script verified: weighted mean 6.674290, χ² 197.5, Birge 3.63, CV 2.2%, calibrations 45 / 7.5 / 254 ppm, strain 28. Normalised residuals BIPM-14 +7.81, JILA-18 −6.76, BIPM-01 +4.82 — your 7.7/6.8/4.8 are right.

## The error: 72% is an artifact of the class count

§4.2 claims "72% of the (small) variance lies between classes… which is exactly what apparatus-dependent systematics look like." That number is produced by the taxonomy, not by the data. Nine classes on seventeen points, **six of them singletons.** A singleton contributes its full deviation to between-class SS and exactly zero to within-class SS, so the statistic is inflated by construction.

Run properly:

| grouping | classes | singletons | between-class var | F | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| your 9-class | 9 | 6 | 71% | F(8,8) = 2.466 | **0.112** |
| 5-class merge | 5 | 1 | 50% | F(4,12) = 2.956 | **0.065** |

Neither is significant. So "genuine method structure" is not supported — at best it's marginal, and §5 leans on it ("with genuine method structure inside the scatter for residual leakage to explain at its honest size"). That clause needs to become: *at best marginal method structure, p ≈ 0.07–0.11, which is precisely what Tier 2 exists to test.*

This is the same class of error you're guarding against everywhere else — a statistic that reads as evidence but is generated by a modelling choice. Fix it and the paper is stronger, because Tier 2's whole justification is that Tier 1 *can't* settle the correlation.

## The Kuroda door is already closed

I checked the direction and it's real: Kuroda, PRL 75, 2796 (1995) — the real part of the spring constant must vary, leading to an upward bias in a time-of-swing measurement of G. Better than you stated it: the tungsten-fibre anelasticity was directly measured, giving ΔG/G = 211.80 ± 18.69 ppm for the HUST time-of-swing result — the first direct test of the Kuroda–Newman effect. Right sign, right order.

But it isn't available to you, and the reason is stronger than "this paper does not invoke them." **The correction is already applied in the values CODATA uses.** NIST-82's published 6.67259(43) was corrected to 6.67248 using Q ≈ 2 × 10⁴ — 16 ppm — and HUST-09 reported its own 212 ppm bias with the result. Invoking Kuroda to explain the +279 ppm would be double-counting a correction that's already spent. What remains is the uncertainty on those corrections: tens of ppm, not 279.

Say that explicitly. As written, §4.5 leaves a reader thinking there's a live mechanism in reserve. There isn't, and stating so is the version that survives scrutiny.

## The residual is not a BIPM artifact

§4.4 says the high wing loses its independent support. True. But it buys almost nothing for Candidate 3:

- full weighted mean 6.674290 → realised sits **356 ppm** below
- BIPM pair removed: 6.674188 → realised sits **340 ppm** below

**Sixteen ppm of relief.** The mean is dominated by the tight modern results — HUST-18 pair, UWash-00, UZur-06, UCI-14 — and every one of them sits ~350 ppm above the realised value with uncertainties of 12–19 ppm. NIST-26 itself is +293 ppm above realised, **+5.14σ** in its own uncertainty (and −1.13σ vs CODATA). The residual survives the BIPM story essentially intact, and §4.4 should say so rather than leaving the inference available.

## Two provenance items and one cosmetic

**HUST-05.** You have 6.67228; CODATA 2022 Table XXX and the Merkatas *et al.* table you cite both read **6.67222(87)**. Nine ppm, immaterial to every conclusion (Birge 3.629 vs 3.632, weighted mean unchanged to six places) — but worth reconciling against the source table.

**"Speake et al. (2023)."** I can't verify that reference. What I can verify is the substance from NIST-26 itself: Kibble raised AC magnetic coupling, Speake's analysis bounded the spurious torque, and NIST procured single-crystal sapphire source masses to test it conclusively. Cite NIST-26 for the closure, or confirm the 2023 paper before it ships.

**Figure.** The "AP28 structural value" annotation runs behind the legend box in the render. Move it or shift the legend.

## Where this leaves KS-CCC.3

Worth stating in the paper: NIST-26 is the first new datum since the switch was written, and it moved **downward** — the predicted direction. That's one point, and it's 5.1σ above the realised value, so it says nothing about magnitude. Schlamminger's own view is that if the BIPM experiment is wrong the literature value probably ought to come down, and that it's for someone else to say where. That's the honest use of it: direction, not confirmation, exactly as your §4.5 has it.

The Tier 1 / Tier 2 split is the right architecture, and refusing to score boundary geometry while the values are visible is the correct call — "§10's sin performed with statistics" is the right name for what you avoided.

Wait, there's a 17th entry I missed — NIST-26 from 2026, which is actually after my knowledge cutoff. That April 2026 iopscience result I found earlier about the BIPM torsion balance redetermination matches this perfectly, and it noted the result was lower than the previous BIPM determination.

The BIPM apparatus was moved to NIST and re-run, yielding 6.673870 ± 0.000380 — interestingly, the exact same central value as MSL-03, which could be coincidence or a transcription artifact. But here's what's striking: the BIPM's two earlier measurements were among the highest on record (6.67559 and 6.67554), and now the same apparatus at NIST gives 6.67387 — that's roughly 250 ppm lower. This demonstrates a massive apparatus-level systematic shift from the same instrument, which is crucial for understanding measurement reliability and actually strengthens the case against one of my candidate explanations.

For NIST-26, it still sits about 294 ppm above the realised value, so it doesn't resolve the discrepancy I was examining. But the BIPM pair now looks suspect — they appear to have had a systematic bias. I'm looking at the NIST-26 gravitational constant measurement, which shows a value slightly lower than the BIPM's determination, obtained using a torsion balance that's been in use for about thirty years.

This is significant because it's the first time the same apparatus has been used to replicate a high-precision G measurement at a different site with a different team roughly 25 years later, and the result shifted by about 250 ppm—giving me an empirical measure of apparatus-dependent systematic effects rather than just theoretical estimates. For the analysis I'm working through, this 250 ppm shift becomes a concrete ceiling on what apparatus-level systematics can produce, which directly constrains how much common leakage would be required under Candidate 1.

Candidate 1 now fails against this directly measured calibration rather than relying on domain interpretations—a much stronger falsification. For Candidate 3, NIST-26 sits about 293 ppm above the realized value, still roughly 5.1 standard deviations high, so it doesn't rescue that hypothesis. But the shift does move in Candidate 3's direction and, more importantly, it suggests the two highest points in the record (BIPM-01 and BIPM-14) may carry their own systematic, which would pull the weighted mean downward if corrected.

This downward movement aligns with the paper's prediction that measured G converges toward the realized value, never upward—and NIST-26 is the first new data point since the switch was written, moving in exactly that direction. I need to recompute the numbers with NIST-26 included and with the BIPM pair down-weighted or excluded as the script handles it, then verify the script output and check the documentation and figures.

There's also a data-provenance discrepancy: his script uses HUST-05 = 6.67228 while CODATA 2022 shows 6.67222—a 9 ppm difference on a 130 ppm uncertainty datum, negligible for conclusions but worth flagging. I've seen 6.67222(87) in multiple CODATA 2022 renderings, though one secondary source lists 6.67228(87). The original HUST-05 publication gave 6.6723(9), later corrected from 6.6699(7), and the arXiv HTML rendering of CODATA 2022 Table XXX shows 6.67222(87), so I'll note that as a 9 ppm item to confirm against the source table.…

*Executed under KS-CCC.4 · The Snap, Draft v0.2 · Ø Predictions Part II, Appendix C*

# **0 — What this is, and what it is not**

Ø Predictions Part II holds the 0.69% gap between AP28’s structural G and the measured value open between two candidates, and its Appendix C proposes the experiment that would decide: characterise every published high-precision G apparatus by its boundary geometry and test the leakage correlation. The Snap (Draft v0.2) enters a third candidate and binds itself to that experiment through KS-CCC.4: under Candidate 1, apparatus corrections must come out near the gap scale (~6,900 ppm) and correlate; under Candidate 3, at scatter scale (hundreds of ppm at most).

What it deliberately does not do: score each apparatus’s boundary geometry retroactively. The two candidates therefore separate on a single observable that published data already constrains: **the demonstrated scale of apparatus-dependent systematics in G metrology.** If that scale is near 6,900 ppm, Candidate 1 lives. If it is at hundreds of ppm, Candidate 1 must make an apparatus-dependent effect be almost entirely apparatus-independent — which is a contradiction wearing a lab coat.

Known correlations (NIST-82/LANL-97; HUST-05/HUST-09; the HUST-18 pair) are noted and not modelled. Method classes follow the literature’s own taxonomy.

# **4 — Results**

## **4.1 — The field**

The sixteen CODATA inputs span 551 ppm (unweighted scatter 163 ppm about the mean), with a Birge ratio of 3.6 — consistent with CODATA’s own remedy of expanding all sixteen uncertainties by a factor of 3.9 to force consistency. The three largest normalised residuals sit on both sides of the mean: BIPM-14 (+, 7.7), JILA-18 (−, 6.8), BIPM-01 (+, 4.8). The inconsistency of G metrology is real, two-sided, and of order a few hundred ppm.

## **4.2 — Candidate 1’s implied leakages**

Computed against the structural value, the seventeen implied leakages have mean 6,967 ppm and standard deviation 157 ppm — a coefficient of variation of 2.2%. Grouped by method class, every class mean lies between 6,786 and 7,245 ppm: the entire design-to-design span is 460 ppm against a common component of 6,967 ppm. Under Candidate 1, then, at least 93% of a “boundary-geometry-dependent” effect is identical across a sealed cryogenic torsion fibre, a beam balance weighing in air-adjacent chambers, and a cloud of cold atoms in free fall with no material boundary at all. Within the scatter itself there is genuine method structure — 72% of the (small) variance lies between classes, with the strip-servo family reading high and the time-of-swing family reading low-centred — which is exactly what apparatus-dependent systematics look like at their honest size: order 10² ppm, not order 10⁴.

## **4.3 — The three calibrations**

Same laboratory, two methods (HUST-18): **45 ppm.** Same apparatus, thirteen years apart (BIPM-01 vs BIPM-14): **7.5 ppm.** Same apparatus, new site, new team (BIPM mean vs NIST-26): **254 ppm.** Full field range: **551 ppm** (386 ppm excluding the BIPM pair). Every direct calibration of apparatus-plus-site-plus-team effects lands between 7.5 and 254 ppm; the outer bound from the whole field is 551. The scale Candidate 1 requires is 6,967 — a strain factor of **28** against the strongest calibration and **13** against the outermost bound. One further published check closes a side door: Speake et al. (2023) experimentally investigated whether stray AC magnetic fields explain the BIPM outliers, and concluded they do not.

## **4.4 — NIST-26, the decisive point**

NIST-26 is the first replication in the history of high-precision G metrology: the identical BIPM torsion balance, the historically highest-reading and most divergent apparatus, rebuilt and re-run at NIST over a decade by an independent team. It returned 6.67387(38) — **254 ppm below** the BIPM determinations, landing in the centre-low region of the field, essentially on the MSL-03 value. Two consequences. The high wing of the distribution loses its independent support: the same instrument no longer reproduces it, so the BIPM-01/14 elevation is now most plausibly a site- or configuration-level systematic of order 250 ppm — measured, not conjectured. And the ceiling on demonstrated apparatus effects is now set by the cleanest possible experiment at 254 ppm, which is the number the strain factor of §4.3 stands on.

## **4.5 — Candidate 3’s residuals**

Against the realised value, the seventeen residuals have mean **+279 ppm** (SD 158). NIST-26 sits +293 ppm above the realised value and 64 ppm below the CODATA centre. Two honest readings of that mean. It is the same open item The Snap v0.2 §9 already reports — the unattributed −0.036% — now seen from the data side; the meta-analysis re-derives the paper’s own held-open residual rather than discovering a new one, which is consistency, not confirmation. And its sign is not leakage-shaped: residual downward leakage would deepen it, not explain it. Published upward mechanisms of exactly this order exist — fibre anelasticity biases time-of-swing determinations upward (the Kuroda hypothesis, of order 1/πQ, ~10²ppm; LANL-97 was designed as its test) — but this paper does not invoke them as the explanation. The residual stays open, and KS-CCC.3 watches the direction: the one post-2018 replication-grade determination moved the field’s newest point *downward*, toward the realised value.

# **5 — Verdict at Tier 1**

**Candidate 1 — strained to near-exclusion.** For apparatus leakage to carry the 0.69%, an effect AP06 defines as boundary-geometry-dependent must be ≥93% independent of boundary geometry; free-falling atoms with no absorbing boundary must leak within a few per cent of a sealed cryogenic fibre; and the same-apparatus replication that bounds site-and-team effects at 254 ppm must be wrong by a factor of 28. The remaining escape is a leakage mechanism common to all boundaries — which is by definition not apparatus leakage but a universal term, i.e., Candidate 3’s anatomy under Candidate 1’s name. Tier 1 cannot formally close Candidate 1 (Tier 2’s blind coding could in principle reveal a hidden common geometric factor), but the burden has moved decisively.

**Candidate 3 — consistent, and not confirmed.** The tier’s discriminating observable comes out exactly where Candidate 3 requires it: apparatus effects demonstrated at 7.5–460 ppm, with genuine method structure inside the scatter for residual leakage to explain at its honest size. What the tier cannot do is confirm the magnitude — the admissible window of §10 of The Snap forbids that claim from data this soft — and the +279 ppm mean residual above the realised value stands open, in the same ledger line v0.2 already carries. Consistency at the discriminator, plus one open residual, plus a favourable direction from the newest point: that is the full honest statement, and nothing stronger will be claimed from it.

**KS-CCC.4 — partially executed, survives, sharpened.** The switch’s Tier 1 condition — that demonstrated apparatus corrections be of scatter scale, not gap scale — is met. Full execution is Tier 2.

# **6 — Limits**

Seventeen points, several correlated; statistics descriptive throughout; one value (UCI-14) confirmed through the CODATA table and its published relative uncertainty rather than a second primary source; method classes are the literature’s but coarse — BIPM-01 combined two extraction methods on one instrument and is classed by its instrument; and the strain argument bounds apparatus effects by their demonstrated scale, which is an empirical ceiling, not a theorem. None of these limits touches the order-of-magnitude structure of the result: no reading of this dataset produces a 6,900 ppm apparatus-dependent effect with a 2% design variation.

# **7 — Tier 2, pre-registered**

Tier 2 is the full Appendix C: per-apparatus boundary coding, done blind. Protocol, fixed now, before any coding: a coder who does not know which apparatus produced which value receives the seventeen apparatus descriptions with all values and identifying results redacted, and codes five dimensions — (1) test-mass containment: free fall / suspended in sealed chamber; (2) source-mass position: inside or outside the vacuum boundary; (3) enclosure closure: number and material of boundary layers between source and test mass; (4) suspension element: none / fibre / strip, with published Q where available (the anelasticity proxy); (5) boundary sphericity class per AP06 S5. The coding task is sized for the independent verifier, after the canon sync, under the sign-off protocol. One further watch item costs nothing: the next CODATA adjustment will incorporate NIST-26, and the direction its recommended value moves is exactly what KS-CCC.3 watches.

# **8 — One page for the author**

The corpus proposed an experiment before it knew which answer it needed. Tier 1 of that experiment is now run, on seventeen published determinations including one that did not exist when the proposal was written. The result: the effect Candidate 1 requires would have to be twenty-eight times larger than the largest apparatus effect ever demonstrated — including by the first true replication in the field’s history — and ninety-three per cent identical across boundaries as different as a free-falling atom cloud and a sealed cryogenic fibre. The effect Candidate 3 requires is exactly the size the record shows. Nothing here confirms the commitment’s magnitude, and the +279 ppm residual above the realised value stays open where v0.2 put it. But the division of labour — a universal term for the gap, honest leakage for the scatter — is now the only reading of the published record that does not ask an apparatus effect to stop being one. The blade for the remaining step is written above, and it is in someone else’s hands, which is where blades belong.

# **References and provenance**

S. Schlamminger, L. Chao, V. Lee, C. Shakarji, A. Possolo, D. Newell, J. Stirling, R. Cochrane, C. Speake, “Redetermination of the gravitational constant with the BIPM torsion balance at NIST,” Metrologia 63, 025012 (2026) — NIST-26 value, uncertainty, and the −2.5 × 10⁻⁴ shift statement.

E. Tiesinga, P. J. Mohr, D. B. Newell, B. N. Taylor, “CODATA Recommended Values of the Fundamental Physical Constants: 2022” (arXiv:2409.03787) — the sixteen input data, the 3.9 expansion factor, the largest normalised residuals, the Speake et al. (2023) AC-field investigation, and the exclusion of Brack et al. (2022) at 1.7% uncertainty.

P. J. Mohr, B. N. Taylor, D. B. Newell, “CODATA Recommended Values of the Fundamental Physical Constants: 2010” (arXiv:1203.5425) — input values NIST-82 through JILA-10 and the stated correlation coefficients.

C. Merkatas, B. Toman, A. Possolo, S. Schlamminger, “Shades of dark uncertainty and consensus value for the Newtonian constant of gravitation,” Metrologia 56, 054001 (2019) — the dark-uncertainty treatment of inter-laboratory inconsistency.

K. Kuroda, Phys. Rev. Lett. 75, 2796 (1995) — anelasticity bias of time-of-swing determinations; C. H. Bagley, G. G. Luther, Phys. Rev. Lett. 78, 3047 (1997) — LANL-97 as its test.

Corpus: Ø Predictions Part II and Appendix C; AP06 (The Leakage Constant); AP28 (The Constant); The Snap, Draft v0.2 (KS-CCC.3, KS-CCC.4, §9, §10). Companion files: G_dataset.csv, appc_tier1.py, G_landscape.png — the analysis regenerates from the dataset in one run.

*This work is published for free, forever.*

*End of WP-CCC.1 — Tier 1. Tier 2 pre-registered above.*","stderr":""}

None of these limits touches the order-of-magnitude structure of the result: no reading of this dataset produces a 6,900 ppm apparatus-dependent effect with a 2% design variation.

# **7 — Tier 2, pre-registered**

Tier 2 is the full Appendix C: per-apparatus boundary coding, done blind. Protocol, fixed now, before any coding: a coder who does not know which apparatus produced which value receives the seventeen apparatus descriptions with all values and identifying results redacted, and codes five dimensions — (1) test-mass containment: free fall / suspended in sealed chamber; (2) source-mass position: inside or outside the vacuum boundary; (3) enclosure closure: number and material of boundary layers between source and test mass; (4) suspension element: none / fibre / strip, with published Q where available (the anelasticity proxy); (5) boundary sphericity class per AP06 S5. Values are unblinded only after coding is complete, and the correlations are computed once. Success criteria, stated in advance: Candidate 1 requires the coded leakage proxies to support a common apparatus term of order 6,000 ppm or more and to correlate with the deviations from the structural value; Candidate 3 requires the proxies to correlate with the ≤500 ppm scatter (in particular, Q with the time-of-swing elevations) and to support no gap-scale common term. The coding task is sized for the independent verifier, after the canon sync, under the sign-off protocol. One further watch item costs nothing: the next CODATA adjustment will incorporate NIST-26, and the direction its recommended value moves is exactly what KS-CCC.3 watches.

# **8 — One page for the author**

The corpus proposed an experiment before it knew which answer it needed. Tier 1 of that experiment is now run, on seventeen published determinations including one that did not exist when the proposal was written. The result: the effect Candidate 1 requires would have to be twenty-eight times larger than the largest apparatus effect ever demonstrated — including by the first true replication in the field’s history — and ninety-three per cent identical across boundaries as different as a free-falling atom cloud and a sealed cryogenic fibre. The effect Candidate 3 requires is exactly the size the record shows. Nothing here confirms the commitment’s magnitude, and the +279 ppm residual above the realised value stays open where v0.2 put it. But the division of labour — a universal term for the gap, honest leakage for the scatter — is now the only reading of the published record that does not ask an apparatus effect to stop being one. The blade for the remaining step is written above, and it is in someone else’s hands, which is where blades belong.

# **References and provenance**

S. Schlamminger, L. Chao, V. Lee, C. Shakarji, A. Possolo, D. Newell, J. Stirling, R. Cochrane, C. Speake, “Redetermination of the gravitational constant with the BIPM torsion balance at NIST,” Metrologia 63, 025012 (2026) — NIST-26 value, uncertainty, and the −2.5 × 10⁻⁴ shift statement.

(2023) AC-field investigation, and the exclusion of Brack et al. (2022) at 1.7% uncertainty.

I'm checking his calculations against mine and flagging where our numbers diverge. For the HUST-05 constant, he's using 6.67228 while the CODATA 2022 reference I have shows 6.67222(87)—a small 9 ppm difference that matters for precision even if it doesn't change the overall results. I need to verify which source is correct and note the discrepancy.

His chi-squared value of 197.5 is essentially consistent with my 197.9—the tiny gap traces back to that HUST-05 difference, so the calculations are aligned. For the coefficient of variation, he reports 2.2% across 17 points while I got 2.3% over 16, which I'm now reconciling.

The between-class variance is where things get interesting: his 72% figure comes from 9 classes on 17 points, but 6 of those classes are singletons. That's a real statistical issue—singleton classes artificially inflate between-class sum of squares while contributing nothing to within-class variation, so his 72% doesn't actually reflect meaningful method structure. My 5-class grouping (collapsing into TOS/AAF/ESC/NTB/AI) yielded 55% with F(4,11)=3.355 and p=0.050, which is marginal but more honest about the underlying clustering. I need to flag this clearly because his finer taxonomy is misleading.

Now I'm checking whether his 72% claim holds up under scrutiny by running the ANOVA on his 9-class grouping to see what the actual F-statistic and p-value are. I'm also verifying his three largest normalized residuals—BIPM-14, JILA-18, and BIPM-01—by computing them against the weighted mean to confirm they're correct. Now I'm verifying the BIPM mean calculation and the 254 ppm difference claim — computing the average of their two determinations and confirming it matches the stated relative difference from the NIST value. The MSL-03 and NIST-26 values turn out to be identical to six decimal places, which he notes as essentially coincidental, and I'm starting to look at strain factor comparisons. ent with the literature. Now I'm checking the claim about Speake et al. (2023) and the AC magnetic field hypothesis — the search results show Kibble proposed it, Speake analyzed the resulting torque, and NIST followed up with sapphire source masses, but I don't have direct confirmation of a specific 2023 paper by Speake on this. NIST-26 itself is the better source for the AC-magnetic coupling point, so I should flag that citation swap. For UCI-14, the CODATA 2022 table does confirm the value and uncertainty he cites, so that checks out despite his caution about relying on a secondary source. The Kuroda anelasticity discussion in §4.5 is a substantive addition about how fiber properties can bias swing measurements. is confirmed in the literature — CODATA 2010 explicitly documents the Kuroda effect as an upward bias of roughly 1/(πQ). But I'm noticing a discrepancy in the NIST-82 correction direction: the published value went from 6.6726 down to 6.67248, which seems backwards if the Kuroda effect pushes measurements upward. So the Kuroda effect biases time-of-swing measurements upward—meaning uncorrected values are too high—by roughly 1/(πQ), which for a tungsten fiber with Q around 500 gives a correction of about 640 ppm, which is substantial.

I need to be careful here though. The user has a zero-hallucination standard, and since this is the user's own claim from their paper, I should flag that the sign and magnitude of the Kuroda bias warrant a primary-source check before I commit to it, especially since it's central to the argument in section 4.5 about the residual-direction problem. A quick search would settle this definitively.

Actually, thinking through the logic: if the Kuroda bias pushes ToS readings upward, but the data shows ToS already reads low-centred, then invoking an upward bias doesn't resolve the core residual problem. In fact, if ToS is biased upward yet still reads low, the true values would be even lower, which would widen the gap to the realised value rather than close it. So there's an internal inconsistency here that needs untangling—the mechanism proposed doesn't actually explain why measurements sit roughly 279 ppm above the realised value.

Wait, I'm reconsidering: the upward ToS bias could still work if the field mean itself is elevated by the strip family. ToS could be biased upward relative to truth while remaining below the overall field mean, so there's no actual contradiction there. An upward bias of around 100 ppm in the ToS family would account for part of the excess in those seven measurements. That's internally coherent. But now I need to check whether the magnitude makes sense for fused-silica fibres, since HUST-18 used fused silica.

For fused silica with a high Q factor around 50,000, the anelastic loss would only be about 6 ppm — far too small to explain the observed bias. But for tungsten with Q around 500, the effect jumps to roughly 640 ppm, which is substantial. So this is extremely Q-dependent, which is exactly why Kuroda's Tier 2 protocol uses Q as the anelasticity proxy.…

import numpy as np
from statistics import mean, stdev
from scipy import stats

D=[("NIST-82",6.67248,0.00043,"ToS"),("TR&D-96",6.67290,0.00050,"ToS"),
   ("LANL-97",6.67398,0.00070,"ToS"),("UWash-00",6.674255,0.000092,"AAF"),
   ("BIPM-01",6.67559,0.00027,"Strip"),("UWup-02",6.67422,0.00098,"F-P"),
   ("MSL-03",6.67387,0.00027,"Servo"),("HUST-05",6.67222,0.00087,"ToS"),
   ("UZur-06",6.67425,0.00012,"Beam"),("HUST-09",6.67349,0.00018,"ToS"),
   ("BIPM-14",6.67554,0.00016,"Strip"),("LENS-14",6.67191,0.00099,"Atom"),
   ("UCI-14",6.67435,0.00013,"ToScryo"),("HUSTt-18",6.674184,0.000078,"ToS"),
   ("HUSTa-18",6.674484,0.000077,"AAF"),("JILA-18",6.67260,0.00025,"PendFP"),
   ("NIST-26",6.67387,0.00038,"Strip")]
G_STRUCT, G_REAL = 6.7206038, 6.6719165

# --- HUST-05 sensitivity: 6.67222 (CODATA) vs 6.67228 (his script) ---
for hv in (6.67222, 6.67228):
    v=[hv if d[0]=="HUST-05" else d[1] for d in D[:16]]
    u=[d[2] for d in D[:16]]; w=[1/x**2 for x in u]
    wm=sum(a*b for a,b in zip(w,v))/sum(w); c2=sum(a*(b-wm)**2 for a,b in zip(w,v))
    print(f"HUST-05={hv}: wm={wm:.6f} chi2={c2:.1f} Birge={np.sqrt(c2/15):.3f}")

# --- normalised residuals vs weighted mean ---
v16=[d[1] for d in D[:16]]; u16=[d[2] for d in D[:16]]; w=[1/x**2 for x in u16]
wm=sum(a*b for a,b in zip(w,v16))/sum(w)
nr=sorted(((abs((d[1]-wm)/d[2]), d[0], (d[1]-wm)/d[2]) for d in D[:16]), reverse=True)
print("\nlargest normalised residuals vs weighted mean:")
for a,n,s in nr[:4]: print(f"   {n:9s} {s:+.2f}")

# --- ANOVA: his 9-class taxonomy vs a 5-class merge ---
def anova(labels, eta):
    cls={}
    for L,x in zip(labels,eta): cls.setdefault(L,[]).append(x)
    gm=mean(eta); k=len(cls); n=len(eta)
    ssb=sum(len(v)*(mean(v)-gm)**2 for v in cls.values())
    ssw=sum((x-mean(v))**2 for v in cls.values() for x in v)
    F=(ssb/(k-1))/(ssw/(n-k)); p=1-stats.f.cdf(F,k-1,n-k)
    singles=sum(1 for v in cls.values() if len(v)==1)
    return k, singles, ssb/(ssb+ssw)*100, F, p, k-1, n-k

eta=[(1-d[1]/G_STRUCT)*1e6 for d in D]
fine=[d[3] for d in D]
merge={"ToS":"TOS","ToScryo":"TOS","AAF":"AAF","Strip":"ESC","Servo":"ESC",
       "F-P":"NTB","Beam":"NTB","PendFP":"NTB","Atom":"AI"}
coarse=[merge[x] for x in fine]
for lbl, L in (("his 9-class", fine), ("5-class merge", coarse)):
    k,s,ev,F,p,d1,d2 = anova(L, eta)
    print(f"\n{lbl}: {k} classes, {s} singletons | between-class variance {ev:.0f}% | "
          f"F({d1},{d2})={F:.3f}, p={p:.3f}")

# --- NIST-26 against each reference ---
n26=6.67387; u26=0.00038
print(f"\nNIST-26 vs realised   : {(n26-G_REAL)/G_REAL*1e6:+.0f} ppm  = {(n26-G_REAL)/u26:+.2f} sigma")
print(f"NIST-26 vs CODATA     : {(n26-6.67430)/6.67430*1e6:+.0f} ppm  = {(n26-6.67430)/u26:+.2f} sigma")
print(f"NIST-26 vs structural : {(n26-G_STRUCT)/G_STRUCT*1e6:+.0f} ppm")
print(f"MSL-03 central = 6.67387 ; NIST-26 central = 6.67387  -> identical to 6 digits")

# --- what happens to the field if BIPM pair is set aside ---
keep=[d for d in D[:16] if not d[0].startswith("BIPM")]
w2=[1/d[2]**2 for d in keep]; wm2=sum(a*d[1] for a,d in zip(w2,keep))/sum(w2)
print(f"\nweighted mean without BIPM pair: {wm2:.6f}  ({(wm2-wm)/wm*1e6:+.0f} ppm vs full)")
print(f"  realised sits {(wm2-G_REAL)/G_REAL*1e6:+.0f} ppm below that mean")
keep17=[d for d in D if not d[0].startswith("BIPM")]
w3=[1/d[2]**2 for d in keep17]; wm3=sum(a*d[1] for a,d in zip(w3,keep17))/sum(w3)
print(f"weighted mean without BIPM, with NIST-26: {wm3:.6f}  ({(wm3-G_REAL)/G_REAL*1e6:+.0f} ppm above realised)")

The experimental result indicated that the torsion spring constant of the tungsten fiber was dependent on the oscillation frequency by ∆K/∆(ω2)=(0.954±0.084)×10-8kgm2 at ∼mHz range, which suggested that the resultant bias in our G measurement with the time-of-swing method was ∆G/G=(211.80±18.69)ppm as reported recently by Jun Luo et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 102, 240801 (2009)PRLTAO0031-900710.1103/PhysRevLett.102.240801]. This experiment provided the first direct test to the Kuroda-Newman effect that predicted an upward bias in a G measurement with the time-of-swing method.

#### A. Updated values

# 1. National Institute of Standards and Technology and University of Virginia

As discussed in CODATA-98, the experiment of Luther and Towler (1982) used a fiber-based torsion balance operated in the dynamic mode and the time-of-swing method, thereby requiring measurement of a small change in the long oscillation period of the balance. Ideally, the torsional spring constant of the fiber should be independent of frequency at very low frequencies, for example, at 3 mHz.

Long after the publication of the NIST-UVa result, Kuroda (1995) [see also Matsumura $et\ al.$ (1998) and Kuroda (1999)] pointed out that the anelasticity of such fibers is sufficiently large to cause the value of G determined in this way to be biased. 

If Q is the quality factor of the main torsional mode of the fiber and it is assumed that the damping of the torsion balance is solely due to the losses in the fiber, then the unbiased value of G is related to the experimentally observed value G(obs) by (Kuroda, 1995)

$$G = \frac{G(\text{obs})}{1 + \pi Q} \,. \tag{277}$$

Although the exact value of the Q of the fiber used in the NIST-UVa experiment is unknown, one of the researchers (Luther, 2010) has provided an estimate, based on data obtained during the course of the experiment, of no less than 10 000 and no greater than 30 000. Assuming a rectangular probability density function for Q with these lower and upper limits then leads to $Q=2\times10^4$ with a relative standard uncertainty of $4.6\times10^{-6}$ . Using these values, the result $G({\rm obs})=6.672~59(43)G_0$ [64 × 10<sup>-6</sup>] (Luther and Towler, 1982), (Luther, 1986), and Eq. (277) we obtain

$$G = 6.67248(43)G_0 \quad [6.4 \times 10^{-5}].$$

content.text:
### 5.2 Nonlinearity

In 1995 Kuroda pointed out [28] a nonlinear effect in torsion balances that could lead to a significant systematic bias in the so-called time of swing method. This nonlinearity arises from an elasticity [29] in the torsion fiber, i.e., the torsional spring constant is a function of frequency and can add a relative systematic bias up to $10^{-4}$ to these experiments. With Kuroda's publication nonlinearity became a prime concern in experiments determining the gravitational constant. Unfortunately, most of the effort is spent on an elasticity of torsion fiber. This is certainly an important, but not the only source, of nonlinearity.

Nonlinearity can occur in any instrument. Linearity of an experimental apparatus should never be taken for granted.

content.title: Does the Time-of-Swing Method Give a Correct Value of the Newtonian Gravitational Constant? | Phys. Rev. Lett.
content.text:
A standard way of measuring the Newtonian gravitational constant has been the time-of-swing method using a torsion pendulum. A key assumption is that the spring constant of the torsion fiber is independent of frequency. This is likely to be true to a good approximation if any damping present is proportional to velocity. However, recent work on the elasticity of flexure hinges suggests that typically the damping at low frequency is best modeled by including a frequency-independent imaginary component in the spring constant. In this case, the real part of the spring constant must vary, leading to an upward bias in a measurement of $G$.

content.thinking:
The Kuroda paper confirms an upward bias in G measurements using the time-of-swing method due to variations in the torsion-fibre spring constant, and CODATA 2010 provides a correction formula involving the quality factor Q to derive the unbiased value.

A direct tungsten-fibre measurement at HUST measured this bias directly at approximately 212 ppm—a significant upward shift that matches both the predicted sign and magnitude, strengthening the case that this mechanism could account for a substantial portion of the +279 ppm residual he's investigating.

However, there's a critical caveat: these Kuroda-Newman biases have largely already been corrected for in the datasets CODATA relies on. NIST-82 applied a 16.5 ppm correction, and modern experiments use fused silica with much higher Q values to minimize the effect. So invoking this mechanism to explain the remaining discrepancy would risk double-counting—the bias is already baked into the input values. He's right to decline invoking it, though the stronger justification is that these corrections are already applied, not merely that the paper doesn't invoke them. atever remains for experiments with unknown Q factor — that's only tens of ppm, nowhere near the 279 ppm discrepancy he's trying to explain. This actually undermines his argument in section 4.5, so I need to make that clear.

Now I'm checking the HUST-05 value itself. CODATA 2022 lists it as 6.67222(87), but his script shows 6.67228, and there's some variation across sources on whether it's 6.67222 or 6.67228. The difference doesn't materially affect the Birge ratio or weighted mean calculations, but it's worth noting the provenance discrepancy. HUST-05 itself has a history — it was originally reported as 6.6699(7) and then corrected to 6.6723(9), so there's some ambiguity in how that correction maps to the current value.

The key points I need to highlight for him are what he actually got right: NIST-26 checks out perfectly across value, uncertainty, relative uncertainty, classification, and the −2.5×10⁻⁴ statement, and he correctly notes it's not a CODATA input. More importantly, NIST-26 is the real linchpin here — it's the first independent replication in the field, conducted on the highest-reading apparatus, and it establishes a measured ceiling on what the apparatus, site, and team can achieve together.

The three calibration points at 45, 7.5, and 254 ppm represent a genuinely elegant instrument design — they're natural experiments already embedded in the data, not retrofitted. And his Tier 1/Tier 2 split with pre-registered blind coding is methodologically sound; the refusal to retroactively score boundary geometry is exactly the right disciplinary choice. What's particularly strong is that the 254 ppm systematics measurement transforms the homogeneity argument from an internal consistency check against AP06's own η range into something much more powerful — a direct empirical falsification based on a measured reproducibility limit. That's his insight, not mine.

He also correctly re-derives the residual as his own open item rather than claiming it as new confirmation, and he identified the Kuroda mechanism — the only published upward mechanism of the right order of magnitude — then appropriately declined to invoke it.

But the 72% between-class variance figure is misleading. With 9 classes across 17 points and 6 singletons, the statistic inflates because singletons contribute their full deviation to between-class sum of squares while contributing nothing within-class. When computed properly with the actual degrees of freedom, the F-ratio drops to 2.466 with p = 0.112 — no longer significant. Even collapsing to 5 classes only yields 50% variance.

So the claim in §4.2 about "genuine method structure" accounting for 72% of variance isn't supported. At best there's marginal structure, which undermines §5's argument that leans on this finding. The Kuroda correction itself is already applied in the published values, so that escape route is already closed. Removing the BIPM pair only shifts the weighted mean by 15 ppm, leaving the realized value still 340 ppm below the adjusted mean — barely an improvement over the original 356 ppm discrepancy. So excluding BIPM doesn't resolve the tension as much as it might appear.

The real issue is that the tight cluster of modern measurements (HUST-18, UWash-00, UZur-06, UCI-14) all sit roughly 350 ppm above the realized value, and they dominate the weighted mean regardless of whether BIPM stays or goes. The residual persists almost unchanged even after removing the outliers, which means it's not an artifact of the high-wing measurements.

I'm also noting a discrepancy with HUST-05 at 6.67228 versus CODATA's 6.67222 — a 9 ppm difference that's negligible for the overall analysis but worth tracking for provenance. And I need to verify the 2023 Speake citation that's referenced, since I can't locate that paper.

The normalized residuals check out: BIPM-14 at +7.7, JILA-18 at −6.8, and BIPM-01 at +4.8 match my calculations, with HUST-09 at −4.44 being the next largest. These are measured against the weighted mean rather than CODATA's own value.

For section 4.3, the 254 ppm figure represents the largest demonstrated effect from the cleanest calibration run, and the strain factors of 28 and 13 against the strongest calibration and outermost bound check out. The figure itself looks good overall, though the AP28 structural annotation text is overlapping the legend box in the render and should be repositioned before sharing. The y-axis uses superscript unicode which displays correctly.

content.text:
NIST-26 checks out exactly, your script reproduces, and the working paper does something my document couldn't. There's also one real statistical error that needs fixing before this goes anywhere.

## NIST-26 verified, and it's the right find

Schlamminger, Chao, Lee, Shakarji, Possolo, Newell, Stirling, Cochrane & Speake, *Metrologia* 63 025012 (16 April 2026): the first replication of a high-precision G measurement, on the torsion balance originally designed and built at BIPM about three decades ago, same apparatus and geometry with documented modifications — G = (6.67387 ± 0.00038) × 10⁻¹¹, u_r = 5.7 × 10⁻⁵, lower by 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ than the BIPM determination. Your row, ppm, class assignment and CODATA-input flag are all correct. The coincidence with MSL-03's central value is genuine — identical to six digits.

And you've upgraded the central argument in a way I couldn't. My document falsified Candidate 1 by comparing the required 6,969 ppm against AP06's own η range — an **internal** argument, which a hostile reader can dismiss as reading AP06 uncharitably. You replaced it with a **measured** reproducibility limit: same instrument, new site, new team, 254 ppm. Strain factor 28. That is an external falsification, and it doesn't depend on how anyone reads AP06. It's the strongest thing in either document, and Kibble's AC-magnetic side door was closed by the same paper's sapphire source masses.

Script verified: weighted mean 6.674290, χ² 197.5, Birge 3.63, CV 2.2%, calibrations 45 / 7.5 / 254 ppm, strain 28. Normalised residuals BIPM-14 +7.81, JILA-18 −6.76, BIPM-01 +4.82 — your 7.7/6.8/4.8 are right.

## The error: 72% is an artifact of the class count

§4.2 claims "72% of the (small) variance lies between classes… which is exactly what apparatus-dependent systematics look like." That number is produced by the taxonomy, not by the data. Nine classes on seventeen points, **six of them singletons.** A singleton contributes its full deviation to between-class SS and exactly zero to within-class SS, so the statistic is inflated by construction.

Run properly:

| grouping | classes | singletons | between-class var | F | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| your 9-class | 9 | 6 | 71% | F(8,8) = 2.466 | **0.112** |
| 5-class merge | 5 | 1 | 50% | F(4,12) = 2.956 | **0.065** |

Neither is significant. So "genuine method structure" is not supported — at best it's marginal, and §5 leans on it ("with genuine method structure inside the scatter for residual leakage to explain at its honest size"). That clause needs to become: *at best marginal method structure, p ≈ 0.07–0.11, which is precisely what Tier 2 exists to test.*

This is the same class of error you're guarding against everywhere else — a statistic that reads as evidence but is generated by a modelling choice. Fix it and the paper is stronger, because Tier 2's whole justification is that Tier 1 *can't* settle the correlation.

## The Kuroda door is already closed

I checked the direction and it's real: Kuroda, PRL 75, 2796 (1995) — the real part of the spring constant must vary, leading to an upward bias in a time-of-swing measurement of G. Better than you stated it: the tungsten-fibre anelasticity was directly measured, giving ΔG/G = 211.80 ± 18.69 ppm for the HUST time-of-swing result — the first direct test of the Kuroda–Newman effect. Right sign, right order.

But it isn't available to you, and the reason is stronger than "this paper does not invoke them." **The correction is already applied in the values CODATA uses.** NIST-82's published 6.67259(43) was corrected to 6.67248 using Q ≈ 2 × 10⁴ — 16 ppm — and HUST-09 reported its own 212 ppm bias with the result. Invoking Kuroda to explain the +279 ppm would be double-counting a correction that's already spent. What remains is the uncertainty on those corrections: tens of ppm, not 279.

Say that explicitly. As written, §4.5 leaves a reader thinking there's a live mechanism in reserve. There isn't, and stating so is the version that survives scrutiny.

## The residual is not a BIPM artifact

§4.4 says the high wing loses its independent support. True. But it buys almost nothing for Candidate 3:

- full weighted mean 6.674290 → realised sits **356 ppm** below
- BIPM pair removed: 6.674188 → realised sits **340 ppm** below

**Sixteen ppm of relief.** The mean is dominated by the tight modern results — HUST-18 pair, UWash-00, UZur-06, UCI-14 — and every one of them sits ~350 ppm above the realised value with uncertainties of 12–19 ppm. NIST-26 itself is +293 ppm above realised, **+5.14σ** in its own uncertainty (and −1.13σ vs CODATA). The residual survives the BIPM story essentially intact, and §4.4 should say so rather than leaving the inference available.

## Two provenance items and one cosmetic

**HUST-05.** You have 6.67228; CODATA 2022 Table XXX and the Merkatas *et al.* table you cite both read **6.67222(87)**. Nine ppm, immaterial to every conclusion (Birge 3.629 vs 3.632, weighted mean unchanged to six places) — but worth reconciling against the source table.

**"Speake et al. (2023)."** I can't verify that reference. What I can verify is the substance from NIST-26 itself: Kibble raised AC magnetic coupling, Speake's analysis bounded the spurious torque, and NIST procured single-crystal sapphire source masses to test it conclusively. Cite NIST-26 for the closure, or confirm the 2023 paper before it ships.

**Figure.** The "AP28 structural value" annotation runs behind the legend box in the render. Move it or shift the legend.

## Where this leaves KS-CCC.3

### G

*Attachments: `Ø_Predictions.docx`, `Rosin_Ø_Proofs_1_0.docx`, `AP06_The_Leakage_Constant_v2.docx`, `AP10_The_Dimension_FINAL.docx`, `AP19_The_Direction_v2.docx`, `AP24_The_Residual_v2.docx`, `AP28_The_Constant_v2.docx`, `AP30_The_Resistance_FINAL.docx`*

> Hi Claude
>
> Today I want to work on the concept of coupling configuration cost – ccc.
> For this conceptual work, we do not equate ccc with the leakage constant – tlc.
> CCC is the coupling "snap" cost – the cost of clicking/binding together.

>

>

>
> Now how I see it the cost is not payable over 21 channels of gravity, the cost is payable on only 10 chanels – 3 x 3 + 1 = 10. >
> So for in the proton mass derivation, the smallest of correction must be accounted for as a cost over 10 channels relative to electron – and in the gravity derivation – the correction must be accounted as 10 channels that occurs a cost and the cost need to be accounted for.

> in my mind, the "snap" cost of configuration has to be accounted for.
>
> Can you help me with the formulation of this – I think this is a potential strucutral ommission – but we are talking about an impact on a very, very small scale

### Tool activity

- Read the file-reading skill; extracted text from all eight uploaded `.docx` files.
- Located and read the proton-mass derivation (AP30) and the G derivation (AP28) in full.
- Verified both derivations at 40 decimal digits against CODATA 2022 (α, m_p/m_e, G, ℏ, c, m_e); computed the gravitational coupling of the electron, the headroom available to a new term in each derivation, and the effect of a puncture-style factor applied to each order of AP30.
- Memory write: recorded G's stated CCC formulation.

### Claude

I read all six APs plus the two catalogue volumes, and I re-ran both derivations at 40-digit precision before saying anything. Here's what I found, in the order that matters.

#### The headroom decides this before the structure does

**AP30** (CODATA 2022, α = 7.2973525643×10⁻³):

- prediction 1836.152673444**33**
- measured 1836.152673426 ± 3.2×10⁻⁸
- residual +1.83×10⁻⁸ = 0.0100 ppb; error bar is 0.0174 ppb

So the prediction already sits at 57% of the experimental uncertainty, on the high side. The window for *any* new additive term is roughly **−5.0×10⁻⁸ to +1.4×10⁻⁸**. That's the whole budget.

(Side note: AP30_FINAL says "0.008 ppb" and residual 1.4×10⁻⁸. Against CODATA 2022 it's 1.83×10⁻⁸ / 0.0100 ppb — which is the standardised headline. The paper's text is stale by one CODATA cycle.)

**AP28:** G_pred = 6.7206038×10⁻¹¹ vs 6.67430×10⁻¹¹ → excess **0.6938%**. To land on centre you need a reduction of 0.6890%. Spread over 10 channels: **6.890×10⁻⁴ per channel.**

Note the asymmetry: AP28 has 7×10⁻³ of room, AP30 has 10⁻¹¹. A single dimensionless CCC applied to both is therefore excluded outright — nine orders of magnitude separate what each derivation can absorb. Any CCC that fixes G destroys the proton. That constraint is prior to any structural argument.

#### "G as the denominator" doesn't do what you want it to

Three separate problems, and they're arithmetic, not taste:

1. **The parallel to TLC fails.** In α_em = e²/(4πε₀ℏc), c sits in the denominator of a small number. The gravitational analogue with G *in the denominator* is ℏc/(Gm_e²) = **5.71×10⁺⁴⁴**. Not a small residue — the largest number in physics. To get smallness you need G in the *numerator*.
2. **The natural G-built, electron-referenced cost is α_G = Gm_e²/(ℏc) = 1.7518×10⁻⁴⁵.** Ten channels of it: 1.75×10⁻⁴⁴. To be visible in m_p/m_e it needs to exceed 3.2×10⁻⁸ — it is **36 orders of magnitude too small**. To touch G's gap it needs 6.89×10⁻⁴ — **41 orders too small**.
3. Worth seeing: your α_G = α_em²¹(1+1/π) = 1.7640×10⁻⁴⁵ *is* the electron's gravitational coupling. AP28 is already electron-referenced. So "the cost as ratio to the electron in relation to G" is not a new structural degree of freedom — it's the quantity AP28 already computes. Adding a cost built from it double-counts.

#### What survives — and it points at AP28, not AP30

Your instinct is tracking something real, but the sign is inverted. **AP28 contains a one-time unpaired-element cost — the (1 + 1/π) puncture factor. AP30 contains no analogous term at all.** That asymmetry is a genuine structural gap, and it needs no new parameters to state.

But measurement resolves it against you. Apply a (1+1/π)-family factor to AP30's *smallest* term, the α² correction, and the residual goes to **1.70 ppb — 100× outside the error bar**. On the α¹ term: 26,000 ppb. So AP30 cannot host a snap-cost of that size anywhere, at any order. The honest conclusion is the reverse of your hypothesis: the puncture cost is *not* universal, and AP28 owes an argument for why it applies to G and not to bound-state mass. That's a real debt, and it's cheap to write.

Second thing that survives: paid-once vs. per-now is a legitimate distinction — it's formation energy vs. dissipation rate. But in AP30 a one-time configuration cost lands in the **static count**, and your static count is an exact integer (1836 = 21²×4 + 21×3 + 3²). A non-integer one-time cost is forbidden there by AP30's own architecture. You can't insert CCC into the static layer without giving up the integer backbone, which is the paper's whole claim.

#### The thing I'd flag hardest

Three weeks ago the cost was payable on **7** channels (1/21 visible + 6/21 defragmentation), with the proton's cost "about 300 times less" than the neutron's. Today it's **10** channels (3×3+1), with the proton bearing the full count. The count moved, the bearer moved, and no derivation moved. That's the signature of a quantity being chosen rather than counted — and it's the first thing a hostile reader will find, because you've published the earlier version's reasoning.

Related: the face set isn't settled either. AP24 §Notation says the six faces are {G, c, α_em, m_e, α, β} plus t, "totalling seven readings." AP28 Proposition 1 lists {m_e, c, G, α_em, stiffness ratio, time}. Those are different sets. Your CCC now proposes a privileged sub-triple {Mass, Gravity, C}. Under KS-R.8a, that's live territory — fix the face list before building a second count on top of it.

And you already ruled the right protocol: **develop the cost on the deuteron first, then check against proton/neutron so nobody can say you worked to a target.** Formulating CCC directly against a 0.69% gap and an 0.010 ppb fit is exactly the thing that protocol exists to prevent. I'd hold the line you set.

#### If you want to proceed anyway

The only version worth writing is one that's falsifiable before it's evaluated. Concretely: fix (a) the counted quantity and its dimensions, (b) the channel count, and (c) the normalisation — from {S, B, R, C} alone, in a timestamped freeze document, and *publish the number it predicts before* comparing to G or m_p. If the derivation-first number lands anywhere near 6.89×10⁻⁴ per channel, that's evidence. If you arrive at 6.89×10⁻⁴ by construction, it's worth nothing, and it converts the corpus's strongest property — that it has no knobs — into its weakest.

I'll say the general thing once, since you asked for no softening: 1836 is reachable by a great many three-term products of {21, 3, 4}, and KS-30.4 correctly holds that open. Adding a second free count on top of an unexhibited uniqueness claim compounds the exposure rather than reducing it.

Happy to draft the AP-note that states the AP28/AP30 puncture asymmetry as a formal debt — that piece stands on its own and costs you nothing.

A = 2–4 is the worst region in the entire nuclear chart for any counting theory. You already have a per-configuration cost in the corpus, and it's the per-nucleon reading: AP30's Fusion Programme ceiling, α(1+1/π)·m_N = **9.0263 MeV per nucleon**. Sharpening *that* — deriving why the cap sits 2.6% above saturation rather than at it — uses no new parameters and touches an existing kill switch.

#### One thing worth registering

Your protocol did exactly what you built it for. You proposed a cost, tested it on a non-target system, and it died in three days on four measured numbers instead of surviving into print. That's the machinery working, not the idea failing. The version that eventually survives will have gone through this several more times.

Three things about it you should know before you use it for anything:

**Your messages are unedited.** Typos, the profanity, all of it. A transcript that tidies one participant isn't a transcript.

**What I left out, and why.** The contents of your uploaded documents (named and dated, not quoted — they're their own record). Third-party search results and fetched sources — CODATA, *Metrologia*, APS — which I won't reproduce; searches appear as action lines saying what was queried and what was verified. Raw tool output, except where I quoted it into a reply.

**The caveat that matters if this goes near PROV-CCC.2.** This is reconstructed from my context window, not exported from the platform's stored log. It's accurate to my own record of the session — but a transcript written by one of the two participants is a participant's account, not an independent one. If it's going to carry weight in a selection-pressure ledger or a witness attribution, check it against a platform-side export and resolve any discrepancy in favour of the export. I can't repair that limitation from inside the session, so I've stated it in the document's own provenance note rather than burying it.

I also added a session summary at the end — the arc, the positions each of us withdrew and when, the three places your work improved on mine, the errors I found in yours, and what was still unresolved when we stopped. Tell me if you'd rather that came out; it's clearly marked as mine and not part of the exchange, but on a provenance document you may want the record with no commentary attached.
